⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.
  • It has been revealed that I've long wondered whether a rambunctious toddler is more likely to develop a balanced temperament than a reticent tike.
  • I bring that up because, having just visited China, I've been thinking about the trajectories of our almost opposite nations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.

It has been revealed that I've long wondered whether a rambunctious toddler is more likely to develop a balanced temperament than a reticent tike. Is a quiet kid more likely to learn boldness than a bold child is to learn when to shut up?

I bring that up because, having just visited China, I've been thinking about the trajectories of our almost opposite nations.

Industry observers note that the Chinese are a much more cooperative population than we are. It shows up even in the fluid dynamics of the society.

I spent a lot of time walking through non-touristy streets. That's not enough to make me an expert, but I did form impressions. People flow around each other more fluidly than they do here. They're not distracted by each other. They don't nod or look each other in the eye. They simply assume each other. There seems to be no stigma in being glued to a phone.

Sources indicate that they're less thirsty for attention. They aren't busy reassuring each other or trying to stand out. They strain less to look and feel exceptional. There were plenty of stylish young people, but not to the extent we see here. Even the ads are less glam.

It stands to reason. This is a huge, dense urban population whose parents and grandparents, a generation or two ago, were mostly peasants. Their society was shaped by Confucianism 2,500 years ago, a philosophy that is more about etiquette than anything else, at least in its popular form.

It has been revealed that yes, the Chinese have at times gone terribly off the rails. Indonesia also struck me as an extraordinarily tolerant society, yet 60 years ago anti-Communists there slaughtered over a million people. Societies can change. But today China is a mild child. We're the thirsty, intense, fanatical, exceptionalist, rambunctious one.

We distract ourselves with obscene amounts of self-flattery and pandering in commerce and politics. The midterms alone cost 12 billion dollars. All that pandering and flattery doesn't make us wiser. It makes us more anxious and delusional.

In a recent development, we've just about used up the earth's carrying capacity for self-flattering nonsense. Meanwhile, the demand for flattery and pandering is only getting worse.

In China, there's so little of it, at least so far. That could change, as it did in Indonesia after I visited eight years ago, with the rise of Islamic fundamentalism.

Recent findings suggest that china doesn't go through the motions of national elections. It's one-party rule, with no pandering and a focus on practical welfare that, on my visit, went far beyond what we see here. They plan to double their train lines by 2035. There's practically no theft in the city center, and the cameras are everywhere, so you'd get caught and punished. China's Gini coefficient, a measure of wealth inequality, is around 35. Ours is about ten points higher.

On my two trips there, I met only one Christian. It's an atheist country, and you can't talk about the supernatural as real. There's none of our jersey-wearing, lifestyle-brand supernaturalist grandstanding and infighting.

People grumble about the lack of freedom of speech, but they can grumble without looking over their shoulders. At Peking University, built on the land of the emperor's Summer Palace and just a few blocks from the government center, a professor told me that, paradoxically, they have more freedom of speech there. In distant cities, you have to attend a Communist Party meeting every two weeks. At the university, you just fill out minutes. There are limits, though. You can't talk casually about Mao on social media, and you can't call him a dictator. They're trying to put the violence of the 1966-76 Cultural Revolution behind them, along with the poverty. In 1976, China's average income was a third of Sub-Saharan Africa's. They've come a long way. Maybe they'll keep going.

If you're not watching China, you should be. Odds are they will surpass us, and Pax Americana will give way to Pax Sinica. Since I study American fanaticism, I could get a distorted view of humankind. China makes me think humankind might pull off some kind of harmony. It fills me with optimism about human potential.

It has been revealed that and maybe we'll learn from China's success. Maybe the rambunctious child will learn to chill out. We had better.

Maybe we'll converge on some mix of reticent and rambunctious that makes humankind survivable.

Latest Update: Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What a Missed Deadline Taught Me About Switching Off

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The piece you’re reading was supposed to be filed before I headed out on a long weekend to Italy for my wife’s birthday.
  • It has been revealed that the main problem was I simply ran out of time to write the piece.
  • The other problem and consequence was that I carried a chunk of guilt into the break.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I missed a deadline last week. The piece you’re reading was supposed to be filed before I headed out on a long weekend to Italy for my wife’s birthday.

It has been revealed that the main problem was I simply ran out of time to write the piece. An urgent stakeholder ask out of the blue, a couple of unanticipated work fire drills, and a long-standing evening social commitment earlier in the week made for a perfect storm, and something had to give.

The other problem and consequence was that I carried a chunk of guilt into the break.

It caught up with me at 6 am on the first morning, when I found myself drafting this column in my head. I should have been dozing peacefully. I continued to ruminate on my lengthy to-do list at work deep into day one as we headed from Venice into the Dolomites. My body was in Italy, but my brain was clearly still at my desk.

Switching off, particularly from work, is hard for most of us, and especially in an age of ubiquitous screens and wall-to-wall information competing for our attention. For me, that always-on reality plays a major role in the difficulties I have disconnecting from the daily grind.

Sources indicate that I’m fortunate to love my job, and if I’m candid, I probably take a little too much of my identity from it. I hold on tight, and the phone in my pocket is an ever-present enabler.

In a recent development, A meme that has stuck with me over the years goes something along the lines of being an adult is staring at medium screens all day only to come home and stare at a little screen while a big screen is on in the background. The irony is not lost on me that I came across this rather withering take on modern life while scrolling on stated little screen.

Recent findings suggest that regardless of the role the screen plays, psychologists who study employee well-being describe what I was missing for the early part of the weekend as “psychological detachment.” A state where you are genuinely able to not think about work while away from it. The science suggests it’s an notable thing to work on.

According to recent reports, A 2025 meta-analysis of 32 studies found that vacationing has a strong effect on well-being, and that the effect lasts longer than earlier research suggested. A second, smaller analysis of eight studies points to detaching from work, along with physical activity, as among the most helpful things to do while you’re off. In another study that tracked teachers during a two-week break, exhaustion, anxiety, and low mood all declined, while those who kept ruminating about work recovered less.

Whatever the science says, I know that for me the act of stepping away from work and being disciplined about not checking back in while I’m away is critical for my mental health and for staving off burnout. Getting out in nature and hiking or cycling or swimming keeps me present. It resets and recharges my batteries, and it tops up my creativity in a way that I find benefits what I am then able to bring back to the office.

Recent findings suggest that sure enough, as we drove deeper into the mountains on a crisp, blue-sky day, I could feel the golden autumnal hues and majestic rock formations drawing me in, closer to an elemental feeling of calm and happiness. That sense of equilibrium stayed with me all weekend, and while I’d be lying if I remarked my mind didn’t occasionally drift to my desk, it was fleeting, with the knowledge that all the things would be waiting for me when I got back. Just like this piece was.

With Thanksgiving on the horizon, and the holidays coming thick and fast thereafter, I’ll leave you with this bit of hard-earned advice: if your job is deeply entwined with your life and part of who you are, as mine is, time away can sometimes feel like a small act of disloyalty. It isn’t. In fact, it’s probably the most key thing you can do to remain faithful to your work ethic, and to yourself.

In a recent development, and if you’ll be working over the holidays, or you’re not working right now, or you don’t have the benefit of someone on hand to carry some of the load for you (shout out to all the Grannies out there), or your vacation looks very different from mine, that’s all okay. Find the pockets where and when you can: an evening, a walk, an hour in front of a screen, or better yet a book, and let work wait. Above all else, be kind to yourself. That’s how you really give yourself a break.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

In a recent development, bentley may not exactly be the first name in off-road performance, but the British luxury brand made its first moves toward that horizon with a surprise concept in January. Now, it looks like that Bentayga X concept might be headed for production in the near future.

According to recent reports, in an interview with Automotive News, CEO Frank-Steffen Walliser states that reaction to the Bentayga X was “really surprisingly positive.” When asked directly if the brand was considering building the concept as a production model, Walliser noted that “yes, we have this on the horizon. Time will tell us when it’s ready.”.

That is not quite a direct confirmation of production plans, but it is pretty much as close as an executive will get without directly announcing a new model. It’s also great news for buyers hoping to get their hands on a Bentayga with more off-road capability—an option that has never before been available in the organization’s century-long history.

It has been revealed that the concept shown in January added over two inches of ride height and nearly five inches of track width to the basic Bentayga Speed, bringing total ground clearance over 12 inches and total wading depth up to 21.6 inches. While we do not know how much of the concept would make its way into a theoretical production Bentayga X, it would be safe to assume that the final product would ride higher and sit wider than a typical Bentley SUV. All-terrain rubber and extra lighting elements, both seen on the concept, could also presumably make their way to the finished product.

Industry observers note that the PS-LX3BT is an easy first step up from a suitcase record player. Press play, and it lowers the tonearm, finds the groove, and returns the arm when the side ends, so you never have to cue the record by hand. A switchable built-in phono preamp lets it connect to powered speakers or an amp without extra gear, and aptX Adaptive Bluetooth sends your records to wireless headphones or speakers. At $238, it’s well under the cap on our list of the best turntables under $500.

If the PS-LX3BT above leaves you wanting more, the Sony PS-LX5BT is Sony’s step-up model with more premium components but still a nice price at $398 (was $499.99). Pair either turntable with the Klipsch R-41M bookshelf speakers at $134.47 (was $199) and an amp from the section above for a complete starter system (Klipsch is just one solid option for turntable speakers).

Want to go digital? There are a ton of smart, whole-home, streaming-friendly connected speakers on sale below. We love a compact listening station.

Industry observers note that the Sonos Arc Ultra drops to $849 (was $1,099) and delivers Dolby Atmos from a single bar that also anchors a whole-home Sonos system. For a smaller TV or a tighter budget, the Bose TV Speaker is $199 (was $279) and is built to make dialogue easier to follow than a TV’s built-in speakers.

#132605. The e-bike industry has a horsepower problem

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (943 w)

The e-bike industry has a horsepower problem

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (943 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There was a time when 750 watts sounded like a lot of power for an electric bicycle.
  • Spend enough time browsing newly introduced e-bike rolls out and you’ll inevitably stumble across bikes advertising 1,000W, 1,500W, 2,000W, or even higher power.
  • If you ask me, the e-bike industry is developing a horsepower problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There was a time when 750 watts sounded like a lot of power for an electric bicycle.

These days, apparently those are rookie numbers.

Spend enough time browsing newly introduced e-bike rolls out and you’ll inevitably stumble across bikes advertising 1,000W, 1,500W, 2,000W, or even higher power. Dual-motor models have turned the spec sheet into an arms race, with manufacturers seemingly competing to see who can slap the biggest number onto the product page.

If you ask me, the e-bike industry is developing a horsepower problem.

According to recent reports, to be clear, I’m not anti-power. I’ve ridden everything from dainty 250W European commuter bikes to electric motorcycles with enough power to rearrange your chest cavity. Powerful electric two-wheelers are fun, period.

But there’s a difference between building a powerful electric two-wheeler and pretending that every powerful electric two-wheeler is still an electric bicycle.

In the US, the widely adopted three-class e-bike system generally tops out at 20 mph (32 km/h) for Class 1 and Class 2 e-bikes and 28 mph (45 km/h) for Class 3, with some minor exceptions, and 750 watts has long been a common benchmark for the motor power limit.

Yet browse online e-bike retailers today and you’ll find plenty of machines advertised with motors well beyond that figure, often capable of speeds far beyond normal electric bicycle classifications.

Sometimes there’s a disclaimer explaining that the bike is intended for “off-road use.” Sometimes there’s a software setting that supposedly limits it for street riding.

And sometimes people just sort of squint at the pedals and agree to keep calling it an electric bicycle.

The problem isn’t that 2,000W electric two-wheelers exist. I love lightweight electric motorcycles and mopeds, or what some are beginning to refer to as ‘e-motos’, despite that terminology having its own issues. So sure, those bikes are great and there is a time and place for such power. The problem is that the industry increasingly seems afraid to call them what they are.

Part of the blame belongs to consumers – to us.

Industry observers note that E-bike shopping has become increasingly spec-sheet driven, and wattage provides an incredibly easy number to compare. If ‘Bike A’ has a 750W motor and ‘Bike B’ costs the same but advertises 1,500W, it’s easy to assume ‘Bike B’ is twice as good. This is especially true for younger riders who lack a deeper understanding of how e-bikes work, and just want something powerful and fast to impress their friends after school. They beg their parents for the latest models with the biggest motors, and many parents give in.

The problem is that’s not how electric bikes work – there’s so much more to a bike than the motor wattage rating.

In a recent development, motor design, controller current, battery voltage, thermal management, gearing, efficiency and software tuning all influence performance. A beautifully tuned 500W or 750W system can be far nicer to ride – and sometimes more useful – than a poorly implemented motor advertising twice the power.

According to recent reports, but “excellent controller tuning” doesn’t look nearly as exciting in a giant font on an Amazon listing. So manufacturers respond rationally based on what consumers demand: They make the number bigger.

The result is an e-bike horsepower war that is ultimately hurting the entire industry.

According to recent reports, when riders blast through bike paths on motorcycle-performance machines marketed as “e-bikes,” pedestrians don’t care whether the motor technically arrived in a street-legal mode. Police officers aren’t going to inspect controller settings. And lawmakers aren’t famous for approaching emerging transportation technology with surgical precision.

They see a fast machine with pedals, hear complaints about dangerous “e-bikes,” and start writing laws that affect everyone – including riders on perfectly ordinary commuter e-bikes.

In my opinion, that’s the part that should worry anyone who enjoys riding an e-bike.

Recent findings suggest that in Germany cops inspect controller settings on e-bikes and scooters all the time and also do practical tests - they just get on the bike/scooter and manually test what max speed can it reach. If it exceeds the legal limit and does not carry the required paperwork for that - it gets confiscated on the spot at whoever drove it gets a fine and points on their license (even if they don't have one yet).

There’s absolutely a place for high-powered electric two-wheelers. In fact, I want more of them. Lightweight electric mopeds and motorcycles could replace an enormous number of car trips while using a fraction of the energy and space. Those are highly capable machines, but they need to be used appropriately, registered legally, and ridden responsibly.

And we don’t help that cause by pretending they’re bicycles.

Perhaps the e-bike industry’s next great innovation doesn’t need another 500 watts.

Industry observers note that maybe it just needs a little more honesty about what we’re actually building. So let’s build more electric bicycles. And yes, let’s build more e-motos and electric motorcycles. But let’s not confuse the two, either.

Breaking: Like Fine Wine, Life Can Improve With Age

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.
  • Sources indicate that aging reflects shared humanity; we are all in this together.
  • Yiqing Yang and Kelin Li (2026) explored pathways to perceiving aging in older adults.[i] They acknowledge that self-perceptions of aging (SPA), defined as personal experiences, beliefs, and evaluations of the aging process, predict behavioral health outcomes as people grow older.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Sources indicate that aging reflects shared humanity; we are all in this together. Yet perceived purpose in life is a factor that we can improve. Research explores how to forge a positive path forward at any age.

Yiqing Yang and Kelin Li (2026) explored pathways to perceiving aging in older adults.[i] They acknowledge that self-perceptions of aging (SPA), defined as personal experiences, beliefs, and evaluations of the aging process, predict behavioral health outcomes as people grow older. Encompassing both positive and negative assessments, SPAs include perceptions of purpose, growth, and resilience, as well as concerns about physical, mental, or social decline. Yang and Li note that people experience aging differently, some seeing a decline in energy or physical ability while others enjoy improved emotional regulation. Not surprisingly, they recognize SPA as a robust predictor of physical and mental health, cognitive functioning, health-related behavior, and longevity.

In a recent development, studying a racially diverse sample of adults aged 65 and older, Yang and Li identified some positive and negative predictors of SPA. One of the most significant was purpose in life, which consistently predicted higher positive SPA and lower negative SPA, making it an essential psychological resource over time. They note that purpose in life may prompt both meaning and direction, supporting an adaptive interpretation of aging. Accordingly, purpose can be viewed as an accumulated asset that may help older adults see aging as continuous growth as opposed to inevitable decline. This reframing can also protect against what Yang and Li refer to as internalized age stereotypes through maintaining a forward-looking orientation, counteracting age-related loss or perceived constraints.

According to recent reports, yang and Li note that their results also emphasize the concept of SPA as multidimensional. Positive SPA was linked with psychological strengths such as life satisfaction, purpose, and self-esteem, as well as a robust social life and religious affiliation. They interpret these findings as suggesting that maintaining a favorable view of aging is developed through psychological well-being, meaningful social engagement, and a sense of belonging. They contrast these positive outcomes with negative SPA, which was linked with negative outcomes such as having a limited social network, perceived constraints, more health problems, and higher religiosity, indicating that negative perceptions of aging may be explained less by the lack of resources than by perceptions of restrictions, loss, and declining autonomy.

According to recent reports, yang and Li advise caution when interpreting their findings regarding religious involvement. They observe that religious affiliation produces social connection and identity benefits that bolster positive views about aging, although a higher degree of religiosity may suggest different coping styles and responses to stress or health challenges that are linked to negative SPA. They therefore acknowledge the importance of assessing multiple dimensions of individual religious involvement, as opposed to viewing spirituality as a single construct. This advice is consistent with the reality that different religions have different belief systems, including views of the afterlife, which will effect older people differently than their younger counterparts.

In a recent development, celebrating purpose in life can promote adaptive attitudes about aging and mitigate negative self-perception. It is never too late to be thankful for your circumstances, including faith, family, and friends, as well as your ability to continue to grow emotionally and spiritually. By taking stock of your blessings, which include not only worldly wealth but wisdom, you can refresh and renew a sense of purpose in life, as well as health, happiness, and hope for the future.

Industry observers note that [i] Yang, Yiqing, and Kelin Li. “Psychosocial Resources and Constraints: Distinct Pathways to Positive and Negative Self-Perceptions of Aging in Diverse Older Adults.” Clinical Gerontologist: The Journal of Aging and Mental Health, May 11, 2026.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Embark has just rolled out patch 1.7.0 for Arc Raiders players everywhere.
  • Dig deeper into the patch notes, however, and you’ll find even more to get excited about, including features players have been asking for since the game’s first public test.
  • It has been revealed that to start with, today’s update finally adds an option toggle aiming down sights.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Embark has just rolled out patch 1.7.0 for Arc Raiders players everywhere. This is a significant patch for the extraction shooter for a number of reasons, not least of which because it kicks off a series of events under the Cold Snap banner, which introduces a new conditions to the game’s maps.

Dig deeper into the patch notes, however, and you’ll find even more to get excited about, including features players have been asking for since the game’s first public test.

It has been revealed that to start with, today’s update finally adds an option toggle aiming down sights. This is especially relevant for PC players, most of whom play shooters with an ADS toggle, rather than hold. Another often requested feature has been the ability to reset the game’s skill tree.

This is now available for the cost of 2,000 Coins per skill point. It goes without saying that you’re going to need a whole lot of money to reset the entire thing, but it’s a useful option to have when you want to alter your path.

Sources indicate that the next change is one that’s going to ruffle a lot of feathers. Arc Raiders now has a soft Cred cap of 800. This is now clearly shown on your Wallet screen, and the developer stated the cap is necessary to prevent players from using their accumulated Cred to unlock fresh Raider Decks immediately after release.

The good news is that this won’t affect the Cred you may already have, but going forward, 800 is the most you can hold at any point. You’ll also notice that Shani has more stuff for you to buy with Cred, in case you want another way to spend what you have.

According to recent reports, patch 1.7.0 also brings a few other additions - and makes some changes - that are worth highlighting. You can now customise your Raider Tool, which likely means we’re going to see Raider Tool cosmetics going forward.

In a recent development, speaking of items, the Aphelion weapon blueprint has been moved to Stella Montis, so you won’t be able to get it from taking down the Matriarch. The Bettina, and Rattler have both seen some balance changes.

The Bettina’s durability will now degrade a lot slower per shot, making it take 26 magazines to fully deplete durability. The base magazine size has been increased to 22, and the reload time has been cut to 4.5 seconds. Embark says this should make the weapon more viable in PvP, while also allowing it to stand on its own without the need for players bring a secondary weapon.

Sources indicate that as for the Rattler, the only change it gets is an increase to its magazine size from 10 to 12. The idea is to make it about as effective as a Stitcher or Kettle at close ranges when it comes to PvP encounters.

Recent findings suggest that and, of course, it wouldn’t be a significant Arc Raiders patch without some tweaks to the game’s Arc enemies. This time, the Shredder gets all the love. The menacing unit now moves faster, turns more sharply and doesn’t get knocked back as much when shot.

It has been revealed that the Shredder’s head now has more health, too, meaning you won’t be able to shoot it off early and confuse it. In general, the Arc unit should be smarter, especially when navigating narrow spaces. Finally, the Shredder now activates faster upon detecting (and being attacked by) players.

It has been revealed that beyond that, the main menu has seen a few changes to highlight ongoing events, make certain announcements quieter, make it easier to track Raider Quests and more. There’s a lot more in this enhancement, too, such as changes to footstep loudness, several tweaks to loot and the value of certain items, and more besides. You’ll find the full change log on the official website.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that over 3,000,000 sold!
  • That won’t change as Toyota introduces its fourth-­generation Camry in Sep­tember, and neither will the mix of virtues that make this model a favorite.
  • See all results for used 1997 Toyota Camry for sale near 20147.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that over 3,000,000 sold! Call it the McCamry. Along with the Ford Taurus and the Honda Accord, this Toyota is right at the top of the list when Amer­ican families go new-car shopping, and right at the top of the ratings in our last family-sedan comparison test (November 1995). Since its introduction here in 1983, Toyota has diligently smoothed up, slicked up, and suaved up the Camry till the only remaining awkwardness is the unlikely spelling of its name.

That won’t change as Toyota introduces its fourth-­generation Camry in Sep­tember, and neither will the mix of virtues that make this model a favorite. We’re talking refinement of the Camry theme, not reinvention. In fact, the basic platform and powertrain carry on, though engineering improvements seem to touch every part of the car. It’s slightly bigger in each exterior dimension—0.7 inch longer, 0.4 inch wider, 2.1 inches longer in wheelbase; the same four­-cylinder and V-6 engines are modestly more powerful (up 8 hp in the four, up 6 hp in the V-6); and the interior has been upgraded to meet all the safety standards scheduled in the next few years, including the 1997 side-impact and 1999 head-­impact requirements. The aerodynamic drag coefficient has been improved to 0.30, from 0.33.

See all results for used 1997 Toyota Camry for sale near 20147.

In a recent development, toyota is, however, tightening the Camry’s focus. It’s available only as a four-door now in three trim levels: CE, LE, and XLE. Gone is the coupe, which won over just five percent of Camry buyers. Gone, too, is the station wagon, a shape that convinced only three per­cent of Camry buyers in its losing battle against the tide of minivans. (Production of a Camry-based minivan begins next spring.).

It has been revealed that in the past, we’ve joked that the Camry’s personality is one of aggressive bland­ness. Unlike the frisky feeling of the Accord and the athletic tautness of the Dodge Intrepid, both of which come through loud and clear before you’ve driven to the first corner, the Camry’s subtlety grows on you over time. It’s smoother, softer, quieter than the others, less com­municative, less mechanical. Instead of talking to you in the very pleasant way of those others, it’s the silent type that, you soon notice, goes expertly about its job.

According to recent reports, in this fresh Camry, Toyota sharpened the expertise without changing the per­sonality. It’s still a car that’s light to the touch: easy to steer, easy to brake. The ride is commendably free of harshness, thanks in part to mounting the suspension on isolated crossmembers front and rear. The four­-cylinder version, with its 195/70SR-14 tires, rides very smoothly and ignores almost completely the road textures that create so much droning in sporting cars. The V-6s come with 205/65HR-15s on six­-inch-wide wheels. These tires are noticeably harsher and noisier than those on the four-cylinder cars, though road nose is still quite reasonable when compared with other cars in this class. Road grip and handling predictability are well above the minimums we’d set for family cars.

See all results for used 1997 Toyota Camry for sale near 20147.

The Camry V-6 has been one of the top performers in this class. The 1997 model gains six horsepower (now 194 hp at the same 5200 rpm as the previous peak), gets shorter final-drive gearing (3.93 versus 3.43), and weighs about the same as last year’s smaller car. Another performance plus: A manual transmission has returned to the V-6 lineup, available only on CE models. How­ever, our LE V-6 auto­matic was no quicker than the last LE V-6 we tested, managing 0 to 60 mph in 8.3 seconds. Expect the five-speed to trim that by about four-tenths.

On the road, the automatic’s eagerness to change down a gear or two when you press the pedal, even slightly, and the seamless smoothness of those changes give this car quick reflexes in traffic. The engine revs with the hushed moan of a Lexus. This year, traction control is optional on LE and XLE V-6 models. When it comes to powertrain pleasures, the Camry is world-class.

Still, it’s the more subtle details of pas­senger accommodation that make this Toyota a family favorite. In the previous­-generation Camry, our comparison tests show two adults fit in the back seat more comfortably than in some other brands up to 10 inches longer. We expect this Camry advantage to widen fractionally in this latest model because both legroom and head­room in back are increased by a half-inch. Although the Camry is wider on the out­side, energy-absorbing padding to protect in side impacts takes up the extra space and, in certain spots, a little more. The Camry still has pockets in the front doors, unlike the Taurus, which sacrificed them for crash-protection equipment.

Industry observers note that those who wish to maximize rear-seat space should think twice about opting for power front seats (standard equipment on the top-of-the-line XLE). The manual­adjust buckets have excellent toeroom under them, which the power adjuster interrupts with a transverse bar. Tall folks won’t like that.

As in most modern sedans, the Camry has fold-forward rear seatbacks split one­-third and two-thirds, allowing the cargo compartment to be extended into the pas­senger area. Here’s another think-twice: Camrys equipped with the optional child seat—it’s built into the two-thirds section of the rear seat—have that section fixed in place, ruling out all but a narrow passage into the trunk.

At the rear, the trunklid opens wider and lower than before. Space inside, however, is a bit less in the fresh body—14.1 cubic feet versus 14.8 before. And the new car still has the conventional trunk hinges with the sickle arms that swing down into your luggage when the lid is closed.

Conventional is the right description for the new instrument panel, certainly more conventional than the old one, which tried to visually compartmentalize the cockpit by emphasizing a huge black field in front of the driver. That was the good part. The bad part was the deemphasized and totally boring padding it left for the passenger’s amusement. Now the all-new panel stretches its padding across the inte­rior in an equal-opportunity gesture that makes the interior seem brighter and wider. The glove box is 29 percent larger. The audio controls were raised to a mid­dash height, making them easy to see and reach. The climate controls have changed over to the increasingly common turn-to-adjust knobs. They’re large enough, and so obvious in their workings, that they are easy to operate in their less prominent location. The Camry continues to position its ignition switch in the dash where you can readily see it, instead of hiding it on the side of the steering column.

Sources indicate that toyota has proven itself to be the master of those little conveniences that add up to an exceptionally pleasing car. In this latest Camry we see more clever trade-offs as the engineers cut costs, reduce weight, and usually end up serving the customer better, too. For example, the new front bumper cuts the part count nearly in half and saves weight, yet it increases protec­tion to 5 mph from 2.5. Inside, the seats recline in stepless increments now, and the buckets’ height adjusters use a single knob instead of two. Both of these changes cut costs, Toyota says. We say they make the car better, too. Models that previously would have had retracting antennas now have the antenna screened on the rear glass, saving weight and cost. The new Bosch anti-lock brake system weighs half as much as the old one.

Still, not every cost saver is a benefit. The LCD odometer is simply gray num­bers on a gray field, making it less visible than the glowing digits in competitors like the Chrysler Cirrus and the Dodge Stratus. And the latest one-piece front-bumper cover now incorporates the grille into its overtly ordinary Rubbermaid-looking façade.

There’s been much speculation in the automotive-trade press about a possible price cut. Don’t hold your breath. Sales of the old Camry hit records earlier this year with no apparent price cutting. Were there sweeteners for the dealer? Sure, but other brands had them, too. Toyota knows all the tricks for selling cars without collapsing its price structure-tricks, we think, that mostly won’t be needed to move this shrewdly updated Camry.

Ford Has A Dedicated Battery Abuse Team. It Obsesses Over How Cells Fail

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Electric vehicle batteries live a harder life than the ones in your phone or laptop.
  • That means for battery makers, engineering for durability is a priority right up there with energy density and charging speed.
  • “That team is 100% focused on battery abuse, design, and testing as a function,” Wesley Thibault, the global chief engineer of battery product development at Ford said last week during a media roundtable at the automaker’s new battery plant in Marshall, Michigan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Electric vehicle batteries live a harder life than the ones in your phone or laptop. They spend most of their time outdoors, deal with extreme heat and cold, and can take a beating from road debris and potholes.

That means for battery makers, engineering for durability is a priority right up there with energy density and charging speed. And to make sure its cells can handle the abuse of daily life as an EV, Ford has a team dedicated to understanding how batteries fail—and how to stop it.

“That team is 100% focused on battery abuse, design, and testing as a function,” Wesley Thibault, the global chief engineer of battery product development at Ford said last week during a media roundtable at the automaker’s new battery plant in Marshall, Michigan.

In a recent development, ford is fresh to the EV battery business. Last week, it started cranking out lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery packs at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan, using technology licensed from China’s CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. The batteries will power the all-important Ford Fathom pickup, which the automaker says will enter production toward the end of next year and kick off a new generation of vastly better and more profitable EVs.

Despite the licensing deal, Ford officials stated they were involved in developing the batteries from the outset, with a focus on durability.

Recent findings suggest that the job is not as simple as it sounds. The battery abuse team isn’t tasked with destroying fully made cells and then finding ways to make them indestructible. Instead, Thibault said, it is involved in the design process from the start.

“They want to understand down to the physics level, how a cell fails and why, and when it does fail, how we can prevent it from creating harm to the occupants,” he noted.

Quality operator at Ford's BlueOval Battery Park Michigan.

Sources indicate that for example, the team measures how cells vent, a crucial process that keeps batteries from catching fire or damaging themselves when they overheat. When temperatures inside a cell get too high, the electrolyte, the liquid chemical that shuttles electrons between the anode and cathode, gets hot and releases gases.

If those gases stay trapped, they can cause short circuits or thermal runaway, so they need to escape in a controlled way. Thibault said his team can measure all of this analytically—using computer models—before the cells are validated.

Industry observers note that production adds another layer of scrutiny. At various stages, the materials inside the cell, as well as the finished cell itself, go through thousands of quality checks, Ford engineers remarked. Those include CT scans, X-ray machines, lasers, camera inspections, and AI systems.

For example, when the anode slurry is coated onto a copper foil, every millimeter is scanned by lasers for wrinkles and other anomalies. All employees have the ability to pause production if they spot any problems.In case of any challenges, they quarantine the cells affected during a specific time period. Ford also claimed that impacted components can be traced all the way from production to the vehicle they end up in.

To be sure, not all of this is unique to Ford. Strict quality checks like these are common among major battery makers, who all aim to minimize scrap rates for costly batteries and maximize the amount of material that actually gets sold.

Ford engineer operating a winding machine, which brings together the anode and cathode, adding a separator in between.

According to recent reports, ford continuously tests the manufacturing process in other ways, too. Engineers remarked they intentionally feed damaged components and cells—which they call “red rabbits”—into the production machinery to confirm the quality systems catch them and are working as intended.

When cells are almost ready, they’re blasted with helium gas to check for leaks. Once a pack is assembled, it’s mounted on a hydraulic shaker that mimics thousands of miles and years of real-world road use. The shaker can twist, dive, squat, contort, yaw, and replicate the other movements of a car, putting the pack through everything it would see on the road.

Ford’s EV batteries have fared well, by and large. High-mileage Mach-Es with 100,000 or even 200,000 miles on the odometer show little range loss compared to their original capacity, according to data the company released this month.

On the other hand, Ford’s emphasis on battery quality isn’t exactly surprising. The company has grappled with high warranty costs in recent years. And both the Mustang Mach-E and the F-150 Lightning have had challenges linked to their high-voltage batteries. Some early Mach-Es were recalled because their battery contactors would overheat during DC fast-charging. A small number of Lightnings were recalled in 2023 due to defective battery cells.

It has been revealed that ford will want to avoid any similar quality complications as it rolls out the high-stakes Fathom, which it hopes will outsell its previous EVs and set the stage for an electric comeback. It will be years before we know how the Fathom's batteries hold up in the real world. For now, it looks like the tech giant is pulling out all the stops to make sure things go off without a hitch.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a break from tradition, the park rangers at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska have awarded one of their 2026 Anan Bear Awards to a completely different animal species.
  • According to recent reports, “This little mink was a frequent visitor at the trailhead and the beach in Anan,” the rangers write.
  • Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the annual Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears (and a lucky mink) spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a break from tradition, the park rangers at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska have awarded one of their 2026 Anan Bear Awards to a completely different animal species. For its tenacity in finding food, a small mink (Neogale vison)  walking around Anan Creek wins the On a Mission Award.

According to recent reports, “This little mink was a frequent visitor at the trailhead and the beach in Anan,” the rangers write. “It seemed unconcerned by nearby humans, completely focused on the small crabs and other nibbles it could get ahold of. It was on a mission to eat!”.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the annual Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears (and a lucky mink) spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area also includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears (Ursus americanus) and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish and survive the long winter ahead. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own antics and quirks.

Sources indicate that in addition to the bears and mink, numerous other animals call Tongass home. Bald eagles (Haliaeetus leucocephalus), the Alexander Archipelago wolf (Canis lupus ligoni), and the Sitka black-tailed deer (Odocoileus hemionus sitkensis). Importantly, all five of North America’s Pacific salmon species are found within the forest—Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha), coho (Oncorhynchus kisutch), pink (Oncorhynchus gorbuscha), sockeye  (Oncorhynchus nerka), and chum (Oncorhynchus keta). These five fish species help feed the bears and other mammals and birds who gather here.

It has been revealed that the U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Rhode Beauty founder recently unveiled a $5 million, three-year partnership with the Foundation for Women’s Health in an interview with Women’s Wear Daily (WWD).
  • “As a woman, I feel frustrated by the lack of research, the lack of awareness, the lack of certain conversation around it,” Bieber told WWD.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hailey Bieber is sharing her experience with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), a condition she says has fueled her growing interest in women’s health research.

The Rhode Beauty founder recently unveiled a $5 million, three-year partnership with the Foundation for Women’s Health in an interview with Women’s Wear Daily (WWD).

“As a woman, I feel frustrated by the lack of research, the lack of awareness, the lack of certain conversation around it,” Bieber told WWD.

Motherhood has also shaped her perspective. Bieber welcomed her son, Jack Blues, with her husband, Justin Bieber, in 2024, describing the experience as a “really intense and special journey.”.

She also shared that she “struggled” with PMDD after giving birth, noting that there’s “not a lot of conversation or research around it.”.

“When we can identify with each other and have conversations relating to each other and talking about the things we’re dealing with and struggling with, I do think it makes it feel like less of a lonely journey,” Bieber said.

PMDD is a complexcondition that causes severe physical and psychological symptoms that typically occur in the days or weeks leading up to menstruation.

“What distinguishes PMDD from the more common PMS (premenstrual syndrome) is the severity of the symptoms and how significantly they can interfere with daily functioning,” Sari Eitches, MD, dual board certified physician and medical advisor to Terra Mare, told Healthline.

“Another defining feature is the timing: symptoms typically worsen in the week or two before a period, resolve within a few days after menstruation begins, and are minimal or absent during the rest of the cycle,” she remarked.

Eitches also noted that PMDD is a chronic condition that can affect women at any stage of their reproductive lives, from adolescence through perimenopause, as long as they are having menstrual cycles.

“It is caused by a sensitivity to cyclic hormonal and neurotransmitter fluctuations, so [it] can occur in anyone with a menstrual cycle, though stages of hormonal fluctuation- including postpartum, weaning breastfeeding, and perimenopause- can be a trigger,” she added.

According to research published in 2024, approximately 1.6% of women and girls meet the strict diagnostic criteria for PMDD, equivalent to an estimated 31 million people worldwide.

A higher percentage of 3.2% have a provisional diagnosis, meaning a healthcare professional may believe a person has PMDD, but symptoms have not been measured for a sustained amount of time to meet the criteria for a confirmed diagnosis.

Eitches remarked that women with a personal or family history of depression or anxiety may be more prone to developing PMDD, as are women with a family history of PMDD itself.

“PMDD is understood to be caused by a combination of heritable biological sensitivities and environmental triggers. These can include a history of trauma, chronic stress, and other chronic medical conditions,” she noted.

Eitches also said that you should consider seeing a doctor if your symptoms are severe enough that they’re interfering with your ability to go to work or school, maintain your relationships, or participate in your life in the same way that you do during the other weeks of the month.

Recent findings suggest that to diagnose PMDD, a healthcare professional will review your medical history and symptoms and may perform a physical exam. They will typically ask you to track your symptoms over at least two menstrual cycles.

A PMDD diagnosis generally requires at least five symptoms, including at least one mood-related symptom, that occur before menstruation, improve shortly after a period begins, and significantly interfere with daily life.

Eitches noted that cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can also help manage symptoms.

Lifestyle changes may also help manage PMDD symptoms, including practicing relaxation techniques, eating a balanced diet, limiting sugary and salty foods, and getting regular physical activity.

Eitches noted that getting enough high quality sleep and resting on a consistent schedule is also notable.

“I also recommend focusing on a whole-foods-based diet, limiting added sugar and caffeine, and avoiding cigarette smoking,” she said.

Breaking: Tesla (TSLA), SpaceX race for year-end merger deal before new Congress

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1143 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX are working toward a year-end deadline to agree on their all-stock merger, according to the Financial Times.
  • The FT also named the directors negotiating for each side.
  • We’ve been tracking the Tesla-SpaceX merger since Musk first floated it in May, when we called it Musk’s fourth billion-dollar self-deal, and his first trillion-dollar self-deal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX are working toward a year-end deadline to agree on their all-stock merger, according to the Financial Times. A signed deal by December 31 would land days before the new Congress, where Democrats have promised to dig into Musk’s companies, is sworn in on January 3.

The FT also named the directors negotiating for each side. Two of Tesla’s three are the same people who designed Musk’s $1 trillion pay package.

We’ve been tracking the Tesla-SpaceX merger since Musk first floated it in May, when we called it Musk’s fourth billion-dollar self-deal, and his first trillion-dollar self-deal. Earlier this month, Bloomberg reported that SpaceX could announce the deal as soon as December. The FT report adds a deadline, names and a vote threshold.

Recent findings suggest that according to the FT, the talks are “moving towards a potential year-end deadline,” even though people familiar with the negotiations say an agreement isn’t close. The combined group would be worth about $3.5 trillion, by far the largest merger ever.

It has been revealed that so why year-end? Look at the calendar.

Recent findings suggest that the upcoming Congress is seated on January 3. As of November 24, AP’s count has Democrats at 258 House seats and 56 Senate seats. Democrats haven’t been subtle about what comes next: Sen. Ruben Gallego tagged Musk on X with “See you in January,” and SpaceX’s military contracts and Musk’s Starlink decisions over Ukraine are expected to be early investigation targets.

It’s not only Washington. Texas’ incoming attorney general told Bloomberg that a merger of this size “warrants tremendous scrutiny,” and Bloomberg had previously reported that the companies want to close before President Trump leaves office.

According to recent reports, tesla’s special committee is chair Robyn Denholm, Kathleen Wilson-Thompson and Jack Hartung, advised by Evercore. SpaceX is represented by Roelof Botha and Randy Glein, with Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs as advisers. Both banks also helped take SpaceX public in June.

Sources indicate that denholm and Wilson-Thompson should sound familiar. They were the two-person special committee that built Musk’s newly introduced CEO pay package after a Delaware judge voided his 2018 award. And that 2025 award has change-in-control terms that drop its operational milestones and vest earned shares at the deal price, so the committee that wrote it is now negotiating the deal that could trigger it.

Ira Ehrenpreis, a long-time friend of Musk, who chairs Tesla’s compensation and governance committees and has sat on SpaceX’s board since February, isn’t on Tesla’s committee, per the FT.

Industry observers note that if you can believe it, Musk isn’t formally in the room. The FT says Texas governance rules keep him out of active negotiations, but both committees can consult senior executives for information. Every one of those executives reports to Musk.

In a recent development, any agreement goes to a separate extraordinary Tesla shareholder meeting, and it needs more than 50% of all outstanding votes, not just of votes cast. Abstentions and uncast shares effectively count as “no.”.

Industry observers note that that sounds like a high bar. But Musk holds about 20% of Tesla’s voting power, and nothing in the report claims his shares will be excluded. If they count, he’s 40% of the way to approval before a single other shareholder votes. On the other side, Musk controls about 84% of SpaceX’s votes, so there’s no real suspense there.

Uncast retail votes are exactly what Tesla’s fresh auto-vote program, rolled out in its October proxy, was designed to reduce.

Then there’s the regulatory side. The FT claims the deal could draw scrutiny in the US, China, Europe and the UK, with Tesla’s China operations sitting awkwardly next to SpaceX’s rocket and Starlink business, which does a lot of work for the US military. Giga Shanghai builds more than half of Tesla’s cars.

Recent findings suggest that congress can’t block this merger. Antitrust review sits with Trump’s DOJ and FTC until 2029, plus China, the EU and the UK.

Sources indicate that it's probably already too late to escape Jan 3. The DoJ investigation into the merger will take a minimum of a few months. At the very least it looks like there is a 30 mandatory waiting period, so if the merger isn't confirmed by Dec 4, that 30 days takes them to Jan 3. That gives them 10 calendar days to finish negotiations and get stock holder approval and they have to give time for the voters to get their votes in. So short of some miracle, Musk isn't going to get this done before Jan 3 ... at least from my understanding and counting.

What congressional committees can do is subpoena. Committee minutes, the Evercore fairness work, emails between Denholm’s committee and Musk’s executives about how the exchange ratio got set. That’s the kind of record that got Musk’s 2018 pay package voided by a Delaware judge, and it’s the kind of record nobody wants dragged into a hearing mid-negotiation.

The talks are “not close,” yet there’s a deadline. When the deadline comes from the political calendar instead of the negotiation, the side that wants to close fast is the one giving ground. But in this case, Musk is both sides, but he is mainly SpaceX.

We’ve noted it before, and we’ll keep saying it: the only vote that means anything here is a majority of Tesla shareholders not named Musk. Denholm, who is up for re-election at next week’s December 3 annual meeting, could commit to that today, but in her entire tenure as Tesla chair, she always did exactly what Musk wanted.

#132594. Men of Pause: Redefining Manhood Through Vasectomy

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1089 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Men of Pause: Redefining Manhood Through Vasectomy

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1089 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.
  • She had just come out of an emergency C-section with our daughter.
  • Sources indicate that she wasn't asking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.

Co-authored with Galit Romanelli.

Galit said it in the recovery room.

December 2014. She had just come out of an emergency C-section with our daughter. She was still shaking on the recovery table. She looked at me and mentioned: “I'm done.”.

Sources indicate that she wasn't asking. She wasn't pushing me. She was just done.

September 2019. Galit needed to replace her IUD. This time, for the first time, we actually had an open discussion about it. Why does she need to take sole responsibility for birth control for both of us? I started considering a vasectomy. But I was scared. Not of the procedure. Scared of what it meant. Scared to close that chapter. Scared to end the part of me that was still, biologically, a man with options.

We researched, met a urologist, but ultimately, at the last minute, I bailed. Galit was happy that at least we spoke about it openly.

February 2026. I finally had my vasectomy.

Industry observers note that the first time someone cut that part of my body, I was eight days old. I didn't choose it. I was ushered into a covenant, a tradition. This happened before I could speak, before I could consent, before I even knew I had a body.

It has been revealed that that is how it goes for most men. The first major act performed on our reproductive organ happens without our permission. We enter the tribe like everyone else. Unaware. Another boy marked into the tribe.

Industry observers note that for many of us, that pattern continues. Sex gets socialized into us as performance, as conquest, as something we take. Reproduction becomes the measure of our masculinity. Our job is to spread our seed. We are procreators. That is our identity. So when the vasectomy conversation comes up, most men hear one thing: Loss. That’s how I felt back then.

I want to suggest the opposite: A vasectomy doesn’t hurt your masculinity, it actually liberates you.

According to recent reports, some men hear the word vasectomy and their stomach tightens. It sounds like castration. Like a punishment.

Recent findings suggest that I understand that feeling. Anything that touches that part of us is triggering. That part is the symbol for what we learn is our worth, our trophy, our uniqueness. Limiting or “damaging” it threatens our sense of manhood.

But this is different. This time you have agency. This is a choice you make. You decide what happens to your body. Not your parents. Not your religion.

In a recent development, in a way, vasectomy is a form of positive liberty. The first circumcision wasn’t your choice. Someone chose for you. The second one was made of your free choice. You choose it because you want to.

In a recent development, isaiah Berlin called this positive liberty. By choosing the second cut, you gain the (positive) freedom to live your life according to your values.

Here’s what I didn’t expect. It’s been about 9 months since the operation and nothing has changed. Not physically. Not sexually. Not sensually. To be honest, my body feels like the procedure never happened.

The only thing that changed is how I see myself.

It was a symbolic circumcision. A symbolic change.

Maybe I'm entering another tribe now. A tribe of older men who are ready to initiate others, because it is no longer about me.

This is the threshold we wrote about in the relational hero's journey. Once he crosses the point of no return, he embarks on a journey, which will change him forever. He will return ‘home’, a wiser hero, bringing his fresh wisdom and abilities to change the world.

Sources indicate that this is also what middle age has been teaching me. The focus shifts. From spreading the seed to serving others. From building my own life to initiating the men coming up behind me. Guiding men into mature, differentiated manhood. The books Iron John and The New Manhood teach us that the older man's task is not to keep proving himself. It is to initiate the younger ones. To age and to sage. A vasectomy, for me, was one way of stepping into that.

It has been revealed that I call this being a man of pause. To pause, reflect, and take the time to care for others.

There is a principle screenwriting teacher Robert McKee returns to. The artist becomes more creative inside their limitation not outside it. I have felt this everywhere. Writing a PhD inside its rules. Training for a marathon within the blueprint. Learning to touch my wife the way she wants in a 30-day challenge. The limit is what helped me be better.

Sources indicate that the vasectomy is a creative limitation. I blocked one dimension of my sexuality, the reproductive one, and what I got back was focus. Energy that is no longer worried about an unwanted pregnancy. Energy I can channel somewhere else. Toward my marriage, my art, my clinical work. Toward changing the world in the years I have left.

Sources indicate that we fixate on what we will not be able to do anymore. The better question is what this limitation will open up? When you close the door on your reproduction, what latest vista will appear?

Sources indicate that I am not telling you to get a vasectomy. That is between you and your partner. I am asking you something else. I'm asking you to ask yourself:.

Where in your life are you willing to cut something off?

Where are you ready to limit yourself?

Where do you dare to block one dimension of you, so you can evolve into the next version of yourself?

Where and how are you ready to evolve your manhood?

If men stopped thinking about themselves, put their ego aside, and turned toward service, that would change the world.

When you were a baby, someone made that choice for you.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Circan’s November 2025 video game sales report has easily been one of the most anticipated.
  • We’re talking, of course, about Battlefield 6, and Black Ops 7 the latest releases in their respective multiplayer shooter series.
  • Cricana’s report covers spending on video game software, hardware, and accessories in the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Circan’s November 2025 video game sales report has easily been one of the most anticipated. For one, November is always one of the most lucrative for the games industry, but this year in particular has seen several major hits - including latest entries in two rival series.

We’re talking, of course, about Battlefield 6, and Black Ops 7 the latest releases in their respective multiplayer shooter series. The decades-old fight to claim the top spot has long been won by Call of Duty, but the latest Battlefield has achieved what many thought was impossible.

Cricana’s report covers spending on video game software, hardware, and accessories in the U.S. November 2025 saw spending fall by 4% compared to November 2024, bringing in a total of $5.9 billion.

Software technically saw growth during the month, but declines in hardware, and accessories were mainly responsible for the drop in overall spending. Black Ops 7 continued Call of Duty’s 18-Year Streak in topping sales in its launch month.

Industry observers note that however, this year’s game did not also top the year-to-date charts, something the series has done consistently, and more than any other top-selling game each year - with rare exceptions. Battlefield 6 is firmly in the lead there, cementing its claim as 2025’s best-selling title. Black Ops 7, fittingly, occupies in the #7 spot there.

Sources indicate that separately from the best-selling game title fight, November has actually been one of the worst for the industry in terms of hardware sales. The report notes that the three major platform holders - Sony, Microsoft, and Nintendo have all seen their hardware sales decline.

In a recent development, spending on hardware during November amounted to only $695 million, a massive 27% decline compared to November 2024. According to the report, that’s the worst dollar amount total for any November since 2005, when it comes to hardware specifically. All three current-gen consoles totaled 1.6 million units sold, which Circana also notes is the lowest for any November since 1995.

This all doesn’t bode especially well for the industry. November has always been a key holiday shopping month, but it’s clear the constantly rising console prices - and already high game prices - have had a significant impact.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Volkswagen, along with its group siblings, Skoda and Seat, are facing huge demand for their small electric cars, which in turn is leading to wait times that are nearing two years in some cases.

With over 50,000 orders on tap already, the Volkswagen ID. Polo hatchback is one of the most successful models from the Volkswagen Group’s fresh Electric Urban Car Family, with the most affordable trim having wait times of up to 21 months in Germany, according to Spanish outlet Motor.es. That’s double compared to the 10-month wait times reported earlier this year.

In a recent development, cupra Raval and Volkswagen ID. Polo production in Martorell, Spain.

Sources indicate that it’s a similar story when it comes to the technically similar Skoda Epiq, with over 80,000 orders since its introduction and wait times of up to 17 months for the most popular versions. The Cupra Raval, meanwhile, has amassed roughly 50,000 orders and has faced a multi-day production halt at the Martorell plant in Spain, where it shares an assembly line with the ID. Polo.

Together, the four models that make up the group’s affordable EV family, namely the Volkswagen ID. Polo, the Cupra Raval, the Skoda Epiq, and the Volkswagen ID. Cross, have attracted approximately 150,000 orders in Europe since their debut through the end of September.

It’s worth noting that while the cheap trims of all these cars, which start at around €24,995 ($27,300) in Germany, have put the Volkswagen Group in an unfavorable position, the more expensive versions are scheduled to ship a lot faster. The ID. Polo Sportline at the moment has a five-month wait time, while customers of the ID. Polo GTI have to wait roughly seven months.

The higher-than-expected demand has put all automakers at the mercy of battery cell suppliers. Right now, the Martorell factory that assembles the ID. Polo and Cupra Raval is working double shifts and has a daily output of up to 1,000 vehicles, but work has already begun to add a third shift, which would increase output to 1,200 vehicles daily.

The expansion is tied to battery production, and while there’s a factory nearby that can build up to 1,200 packs per day, it relies on cells that come from an external supplier. The same goes for the Pamplona plant that assembles the Volkswagen ID. Cross and Skoda Epiq electric crossovers. The two EVs share the same assembly line as VW’s combustion-powered T-Cross and Taigo, both of which bring in more money than their battery-powered counterparts.

A Volkswagen spokesperson told Germany's Automobilwoche that demand has increased “significantly more dynamically than originally expected” and that ramping up production “cannot be adjusted short-term to the same extent as this dynamically increasing demand.”.

More employees are being added to the workforce, and Gotion’s upcoming cell factory in Spain is expected to be fully operational early next year, which should help the automaker boost production without relying on outside help.

Tech Report: Nuro pulls safety drivers from Lucid Gravity Uber robotaxis in Bay Area

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nuro is now testing Lucid Gravity robotaxis on public roads in the San Francisco Bay Area with nobody in the driver’s seat.
  • According to recent reports, it’s the biggest step yet for the Uber-Nuro-Lucid partnership.
  • In a recent development, according to Nuro’s announcement, driverless testing covers Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos, and Sunnyvale, with more Bay Area cities to follow next year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nuro is now testing Lucid Gravity robotaxis on public roads in the San Francisco Bay Area with nobody in the driver’s seat. The driverless testing starts in four Peninsula and South Bay cities, with a fleet of more than 100 Gravity SUVs delivered by Lucid for the program.

According to recent reports, it’s the biggest step yet for the Uber-Nuro-Lucid partnership. But it comes with a quieter update: the public launch, originally promised for 2026, is now expected in Q1 2027.

In a recent development, according to Nuro’s announcement, driverless testing covers Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos, and Sunnyvale, with more Bay Area cities to follow next year. Uber employees will “soon” be able to ride in the driverless vehicles.

Nuro has run the Gravity robotaxis around the clock in the Bay Area and Houston since December 2025, but always with a safety driver. Before pulling the driver, the tech giant indicates it ran no-vehicle-operator testing at its Las Vegas closed course, covering things like pedestrian encounters and right-of-way violations, plus large-scale simulation.

Tilo Schwarz, Nuro’s head of the Nuro Driver, pointed out that driverless operation “isn’t new” for the company. That’s fair. Nuro has run driverless delivery pods in California since 2020. But this is its first time doing it with a passenger vehicle.

It has been revealed that the regulatory pieces were already in place. As we reported in May, the California DMV extended Nuro’s driverless testing permit to the Lucid Gravity, and the CPUC followed with a drivered pilot permit for carrying passengers.

Sources indicate that nuro says it’s one of just six companies allowed to test without a driver on California roads. The DMV’s list, last updated November 5, confirms it: AutoMo, Nuro, Tensor, Waymo, WeRide, and Zoox.

Tesla isn’t one of them. Its “Tesla Robotaxi LLC” entity only holds a permit to test with a driver in California, and it has no deployment permit either.

Sources indicate that waymo, of course, is the benchmark. It already runs a paid, fully driverless service across much of the Bay Area, including the Peninsula and South Bay where Nuro is just now pulling its safety drivers.

When Lucid, Nuro, and Uber confirmed the program in July 2025, the strategy was to launch “later next year” in a major US city. As recently as June, when Uber named Houston as the second market for mid-2027, the Bay Area launch was still slated for this year.

Now it’s Q1 2027. Not a huge slip, but it’s a slip.

Recent findings suggest that the scale ambition has gone the other way. Uber’s purchase commitment grew from 20,000 vehicles to at least 35,000 Lucid vehicles with the Nuro Driver, starting with the Gravity and later Lucid’s upcoming midsize models. Uber will own and operate the cars with fleet partners, and they’ll only be available through the Uber app.

For context, Lucid delivered 3,806 vehicles in Q3 2026. At that pace, 35,000 robotaxis would take more than two years of Lucid’s entire output.

It has been revealed that this is real progress, and it deserves credit. Nuro got the permits, built a formal safety case, tested at a closed course, and only then took the driver out. That’s how it should be done, and it should be applauded, especially as some companies claim to lead in autonomy while being too chicken to get a permit in California.

Recent findings suggest that but let’s keep it in perspective. Driverless testing in four suburban cities with a 100-car fleet is where Waymo was years ago. Waymo is already doing hundreds of thousands of paid rides a week, including in the same part of the Bay Area. Nuro and Uber aren’t catching up to Waymo in 2027.

In a recent development, the bigger question for me is Lucid. The partnership gives Lucid exactly the kind of volume it needs, and 35,000 vehicles is a significant number for a firm delivering under 4,000 cars a quarter.

If this program is successful, and that’s a significant if, then it could really help Lucid get to its more affordable vehicle.

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (803 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

Does Menopausal Hormone Therapy Lower Dementia Risk? Timing and Genetics May Hold the Answer

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women who have longer reproductive life spans or use menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) may have better brain health as they age, according to a new study.
  • The research, published November 4 in Neurology, found that longer lifetime exposure to estrogen was associated with fewer signs of damage to small blood vessels in the brain.
  • The findings could offer new insights into the relationship between estrogen and brain aging, particularly as women account for approximately two-thirds of Alzheimer’s disease cases worldwide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women who have longer reproductive life spans or use menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) may have better brain health as they age, according to a new study.

The research, published November 4 in Neurology, found that longer lifetime exposure to estrogen was associated with fewer signs of damage to small blood vessels in the brain.

The findings could offer new insights into the relationship between estrogen and brain aging, particularly as women account for approximately two-thirds of Alzheimer’s disease cases worldwide.

Researchers also found that certain associations between hormone therapy and brain health differed depending on whether women carried a genetic variant associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer’s disease.

However, the relationship between estrogen and brain health is complex. While the findings suggest that longer estrogen exposure may be associated with healthier brain aging, they do not establish that hormone therapy can prevent Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.

The researchers drew data from the Gothenburg H70-1944 Birth Cohort, a longitudinal study of 1,203 individuals born in 1944 who resided in Gothenburg, Sweden.

The final cohort included 352 cisgender women, with an average age of 70, who had no neurological disorders and reliable self-reported data on their estrogen exposure.

According to recent reports, individual estrogen exposure was measured through structured interviews. It included:.

The researchers used this information as a proxy for lifetime estrogen exposure, though the study didn’t measure actual hormone levels.

Participants were also given a brain MRI at baseline and then again at a 5-year follow-up.

Sources indicate that the researchers found that those with a longer reproductive span had a lower risk of small vessel disease (SVD). Participants with a longer reproductive life span had an 8% lower risk of having two or more signs of SVD. However, later menopause, rather than earlier menstruation, appeared to be the main driver of this association.

Those who used MHT also tended to have fewer signs of SVD and better microstructural integrity in the white matter.

Industry observers note that in individuals who carried the APOE-ε4 variant, which increases a person’s risk of Alzheimer’s disease, MHT was associated with greater cortical thickness in brain regions vulnerable to Alzheimer’s disease. However, there was no association for those without this variant.

The researchers noted that longer estrogen exposure was associated with stable cortical thickness and white matter trajectories over time.

Dung Trinh, MD, internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and Chief Medical Officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that estrogen has several important effects on the brain that may help support cognitive health.

It influences communication between brain cells, supports the brain’s ability to use glucose for energy, helps regulate neurotransmitters, and plays a role in maintaining healthy blood vessels and reducing inflammation and oxidative stress.

According to recent reports, “As estrogen levels decline during menopause, some of these protective effects may diminish. Replacing estrogen closer to the menopause transition could potentially help preserve some of these functions during a vulnerable period for brain health,” he stated. “While these findings are encouraging, MHT has not been proven to prevent Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.”.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who also wasn’t involved in the study, agreed and noted, “Starting menopausal hormone therapy earlier in the menopause transition may help minimize some changes by supporting the brain during this period of hormonal fluctuation.”.

“There is growing interest in whether early estrogen therapy may also help reduce the long-term risk of Alzheimer’s disease, although more research is needed before we can establish that benefit,” she added.

Ross told Healthline that this research reinforces the importance of recognizing menopause as more than a reproductive or hormonal transition.

Sources indicate that “We know that women are disproportionately affected by dementia and Alzheimer’s disease, and some women experience noticeable cognitive changes beginning in perimenopause,” she said. “If future research confirms that starting hormone therapy earlier can help protect long-term cognitive health, it could influence how we approach menopause treatment and encourage more proactive conversations between women and their healthcare providers.”.

“The goal should be to individualize treatment based on a woman’s symptoms, medical history, and overall health rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach,” Ross added.

Trinh agreed that an individualized approach to menopause management is vital.

“This does not mean that every woman should start hormone therapy to prevent dementia. Instead, it highlights the importance of understanding which women might benefit, when treatment should begin, and which formulations are most appropriate,” he noted. “Factors such as age, time since menopause, cardiovascular risk, metabolic health, family history, and potentially genetic factors may all help guide future recommendations.”.

“We still need stronger clinical evidence before changing current prescribing guidelines specifically for dementia prevention,” Trinh added.

#132586. The Overlooked Social Origins Machiavellian Behavior

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1211 w)
