The Overlooked Social Origins Machiavellian Behavior

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1211 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.
  • Sources indicate that in 1532, statesman Niccolo Machiavelli's book The Prince was published across Renaissance Italy.
  • In a recent development, many philosophers before and after Machiavelli emphasized people as having a self-interested nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.

Sources indicate that in 1532, statesman Niccolo Machiavelli's book The Prince was published across Renaissance Italy. While controversial, his magnum opus on statecraft was widely deemed innovative for de-emphasizing ethical norms and ultra-pragmatically explaining what leaders should do to hold and gain power.

In a recent development, many philosophers before and after Machiavelli emphasized people as having a self-interested nature. Like him, they often emerged from ceaselessly unstable, war-prone milieus. Legalists from ancient China viewed Confucians as too morally idealistic; early modern England's Thomas Hobbes held a dimmer view of human nature than did John Locke. Yet, it was the term "Machiavellian" that endured and evolved in English writing since the mid-1500s. Today, it refers to being calculated, insincere, and even unprincipled to gain something.

Recent findings suggest that as a psychological concept, "Machiavellianism" is associated with cynical, manipulative, and self-serving tendencies. Psychologists have even measured it through scales like the MACH-IV and Five-Factor Machiavellianism Inventory. Popular articles and videos abound with titles about how to find "narcissists" among partners, or to beware of "dark triad" traits in co-workers. Whether or not they capture phenomenologically valid constructs, or align with how health professionals use these terms, they do not always include structural approaches and takeaways. Could how Machiavellianism presents in societies give clues into broader social concerns needing addressing?

People with similar childhood adversities can grow up to have very different worldviews. However, for some, a combination of early deprivations, caregiver modeling, and hereditary factors can increase their likelihood of internalizing cynical outlooks. These could crystallize into enduring, Machiavellian patterns of interaction later on. Early childhood attachment disruptions, relational losses, and conditional, inconsistent affection can contribute to understanding relationships as ultimately transactional. Frequent bullying, abuse, or social injustices without accountability might misguide some to view ethical and, sometimes, institutional rules as naive or frivolous.

Industry observers note that later, resulting cravings for "omnipotent control" can lead to great efforts to control how most others view and treat oneself, sometimes in ways contradictory to one's actual self. One applies an astute "theory of mind" for envisioning what others want. Consider a group leader who speaks frequently of uplifting and bringing people together, but privately gossips and plays potential competitors against each other. Or a colleague who cultivates a reputation as a light-hearted jokester, but emotionally abuses their partner at home. Their friends might not believe they have such dissonant traits, let alone have suspected these early on. Indeed, psychoanalysts refer to the superego lacunae of otherwise upstanding people who harbor deeply dark tendencies in specific domains of life.

But how useful is it, really, to focus on the sensationalism, the individual "wrongness" or "pathology," or the developmental roots of Machiavellian characteristics? Nobody denies that manipulation and relational aggression happen. Individuals with such traits--or at least a strong disposition to them--exist in all human societies, but how and to what extent these manifest depends greatly on one's present and future environments.

Industry observers note that historian E.P. Thompson examined the moral economy of everyday Englishmen in the 1700s, focusing on nuanced motivations of bread riots beyond hunger itself. As Thompson's work supported, people may be at least as driven to drastic action--in his examples, selective intimidation and aggression toward middlemen--by perceived violations of what is normatively reasonable and fair, than by economic inequality in and of itself.

Yet, unlike for his early modern examples, vigilante retribution is no longer as tolerated in most societies. "Fighting fire [i.e. injustices] with fire" can nowadays land people in prison, depending on their methods. Cynicism may then simmer if people see widespread violation of implicit norms of fairness without meaningful consequences.

Examples appear painfully difficult for the observer to challenge; they range from deliberate decisions, like leaders' rewarding betrayals of colleagues who find themselves in hard times, to rigidly structural imbalances like co-workers getting overlooked for opportunities due to their ethnicity, gender, or religion. In turn, self-serving, insincere, performative, and manipulative behaviors can become gradually more tolerated, rewarded, and normalized in groups. Generalized trust, authenticity, good-faith charity, and optimism might all slowly wither.

Is it useful to think of widespread Machiavellianism as mutually reinforcing and cyclically associated with greater cynicism in a society? Maybe yes, but that is also not the full picture. Perhaps in most cases, prone to quid pro quo exchanges and transactional alliance-building, Machiavellianism is unlikely to improve social complications long-term. It would not benefit any group's already low-trust culture, declining public confidence in a given institution, or corruption. If anything, the rewarding of one's playing dirty could encourage more of such tendencies in their circles via social learning.

Yet, for some others, witnessing Machiavellianism's normalization might not transform their personalities overall. It would instead outwardly modify their interpersonal approaches to achieving pre-existing, potentially socially constructive goals. These ends, regardless of their means, go beyond everyday self-preservation and range from improving the marginalized social status of one's group to advancing a specific policy.

It has been revealed that what might such Machiavellian-like adaptation or imitation look like for someone who did not grow up with overtly congruent traits? Examples include adopting more guardedness and suspicion, calculation and self-restraint in what one notes and to whom, flattery, selectively concealing one's true feelings, and discreetly discerning colleagues' interests and "agendas." Saying things one does not fully mean or feel may seem advantageous, even encouraged, when one assumes their superiors do the same. One might increasingly rationalize their strategic exploitation of others' misfortunes. If these are the prevailing, implicit rules of engagement in one's organizational or workplace politics, then so they will practice them. As with what Friedrich Nietzsche said about fighting monsters, they should also take care lest they essentially "become" Machiavellian through and through.

According to recent reports, not every instance of Machiavellianism in one's workplace, organization, or community indicates a structurally sick society. A few individuals, regardless of how much privilege they have, can still demonstrate such features during periods of widespread optimism and trust, even if their tendencies are more the exception than the norm. Conversely, not everyone who has developed a protective cynicism wants to take advantage of others.

That stated, how prevalent Machiavellianism is in a group at a given time may hint at underlying competition over resources perceived as both finite and unfairly allocated. Resources are not necessarily just material wealth, but also social capital, status, and power. Underhanded ways of interaction may reflect not just neurodevelopmental predispositions but also, for those who are most angry, disillusioned, or hardened, an instrumental means of efficiently accumulating such resources.

None of this absolves the need for accountability and responsibility for inflicting interpersonal harms. Advocacy can be done primarily through good-faith methods. Leaders can promote workplace cultures that are more fair and transparent than what they knew in the past. Yet, so long as racism, sexism, xenophobia, homophobia, and other social ills persist, Machiavellianism may continue to appear to some a legitimate way of navigating work and life--not just for those seeking to maintain great privilege, but also, and perhaps especially, for many people without much of it.

Newly introduced Zealand’s Twin-Engine Toyota Celica Is Essentially Unstoppable

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1149 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the art of modifying cars is gleefully rule-free.
  • Wadsworth’s twin-engine Toyota Celica has made literal waves on social video in the past few weeks, as the Christchurch resident demonstrated its remarkable wading abilities in a series of viral videos.
  • Sources indicate that with so many moving parts, Wadsworth went analog with the controls; a pulley system attached to the original clutch pedal also operates the clutch for the rear transmission, and the throttle pedal is divided into an upper portion for the front engine and a lower portion for the rear engine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the art of modifying cars is gleefully rule-free. Sure, there are never-ending hoops to jump through for street legality, but actually building your perfect vehicle is merely a matter of dreams. For Kiwi Gareth Wadsworth, who goes by @garethcars on social media, those dreams meant stuffing two engines and two transmissions into a single sixth-generation Toyota Celica. Seems easy enough, right?

Wadsworth’s twin-engine Toyota Celica has made literal waves on social video in the past few weeks, as the Christchurch resident demonstrated its remarkable wading abilities in a series of viral videos. The basic recipe is a pair of Toyota’s 2.0-liter 3S-GE engines—one mounted in the front and one mounted in the rear—mated to a pair of manual transmissions and fed to individual differentials.

Sources indicate that with so many moving parts, Wadsworth went analog with the controls; a pulley system attached to the original clutch pedal also operates the clutch for the rear transmission, and the throttle pedal is divided into an upper portion for the front engine and a lower portion for the rear engine. If you press directly in the middle of the accelerator, both engines will rev up (somewhat) in sync. Wadsworth emphasized that it is two completely separate drivetrains that require two of everything (two batteries, two fuel tanks, two ECUs, two radiators) and can be driven separately or simultaneously.

But this Celica build wasn’t always this extreme. In fact, the initial version was supposed to be a simple overlanding setup for a university off-road club trip in 2020. He initially off-roaded the Celica with a simple four-inch lift kit and 31-inch tires, but Wadsworth wanted to try something more extreme—and he didn’t want to abandon the existing platform.

According to recent reports, “I had this Celica that I bought crashed, and I didn't have anything to do with it. I was a student. I didn't have the money for a four-wheel-drive, so I ended up building it into a four-wheel-drive,” Wadsworth noted to Road & Track. “I paid $800 for the car, and then I sold the wheels and tires that were on it. So it was effectively a free car just sitting around, and I got some suspension left over from other projects that I threw in it, and the engine came from a crashed car I found upside down off the side of the road.”.

After a year of mud-slinging fun, Wadsworth decided to go all-in on the dual-engine swap. The rear engine transplant only took two weeks, with most of the work happening after school and during a series of all-nighters. A day or two after the build was complete, Wadsworth and friends trailered the dual-engine Celica to an off-road area and began testing its abilities. Some limitations were rapidly revealed.

According to recent reports, “It was just the stock intakes for a few trips. It did have a snorkel on the outside for the front engine. Once it was twin-engine, it had enough power that we could hit the water faster, and that meant that the bow wave would keep going over the roof and filling the front engine's snorkel. We had one trip on the White Bear River that was in flood, and we hydrolocked the front engine twenty-three times, and we got sick of having to pull the spark plugs out, blasting the water out, and trying to get it running again. And so that's why I moved the intake to the glove box,” Wadsworth stated.

In a recent development, wading is one of the twin-engine Celica’s best tricks, as it is fast enough to glide onto the water and light enough to float through. The Celica has floated through currents that have sunk heavier 4x4 trucks, Wadsworth noted. But the twin-engine Celica doesn’t just excel at water crossings, either. Because the gearboxes run independently, Wadsworth can tune the gear ratios of either end to suit his needs.

Recent findings suggest that “There's no weird handling from the differences between the front and rear. It's just whichever engine's got the least load on it speeds up to catch up with the other one. They're effectively a fifty-fifty split,” Wadsworth said. “Because of the biasing, I quite often run almost exclusively rear-wheel-drive, and I only add front when I need it for traction. It's quite a unique feeling. It's so much fun, and probably the main reason I've still got it is being able to dynamically shift between front, rear, or four-wheel-drive and throttle biasing on the fly. In a mud pit, I can sit around doing donuts with the front in neutral, and then I can put the front-end gear in and let the clutch out slowly on the front to transition from donuts to power slides.”.

And it isn’t even too hard to drive—relatively speaking. Wadsworth said that his mates can hop in and romp it with minimal coaching, at least in this configuration. Shifting the two gearboxes can get awkward, but the rear transmission shifter is placed near the traditional shifter, so you don’t have to reach far. Before the pulley clutch system, Wadsworth wired the rear clutch through the parking brake, which required a gentle touch to keep from stalling.

In a recent development, but it wasn’t always so accommodating. “On the original build, we didn't have time to connect any of the controls, so it had two drivers back then. And we didn't have a throttle, so the strap for tightening the hood was tied onto the rearview mirror and back to the rear throttle body, and you pulled it like a train horn,” Wadsworth stated. “We certainly had a lot of difficulty driving it when we first built it, because it required two people to communicate—but it didn't have any exhaust, so we couldn't hear each other, and we had no total control on the rear; it was either fully on or fully off. And you had to get up out of your seat, turn around, and put it in gear for the rear engine.”.

Industry observers note that even after six years of ownership and five years with two engines, Wadsworth plans to continue driving the twin-engine Celica as long as possible. Initially, he considered adding four-wheel steering using a power steering motor from a Nissan Leaf, but he stated the time under the knife wouldn’t be worth it. The more time spent off-road, the better.

Recent findings suggest that A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

She arrives alongside her sidekick, Bangboo Sprout, who keeps with her swordplay theme by calling down flying swords.

Recent findings suggest that zhao is the other playable Agent as mentioned, an S-Rank Ice Defence legend. Zhao is a fast and nimble attacker who uses her giant greataxe to suppress enemies. Zhao can trigger Ether Veil: Wellspring by using Frostbite she accumulates, which buffs the entire squad.

Recent findings suggest that narratively, this particular chapter will reveal the fate of Waifei Peninsula. The quest is gonna take the squad deeper into the Lumite Mine ruins, and the fresh Perception Technique is how you’ll uncover the answers hidden within.

Industry observers note that you’ll be able to pick from Alice, Soldier 0 – Anby, or Astra. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD rolled out the third-generation Tang, a large, high-tech five-seat flagship electric SUV, starting at under $30,000 in China.

The newly introduced third-gen Tang is positioned below the Great Tang, or “Da Tang” as it’s called in China, BYD’s larger seven-seat flagship SUV in its Dynasty lineup.

Recent findings suggest that BYD held a launch event for its fresh flagship five-seat electric SUV on Tuesday. The third-gen Tang is available in three variants: standard Premium, Laser Premium, and Laser Flagship.

All versions come standard with rear-wheel drive (RWD), but buyers can upgrade the Laser Flagship model with an optional all-wheel-drive (AWD) steer-by-wire package for an extra 20,000 yuan ($3,000).

Prices for the standard Tang Premium start at 187,900 yuan, or about $28,000, significantly lower than its pre-sale price of 225,000 yuan ($34,000).

The Laser Premium and Laser Flagship models start at 207,900 yuan and 219,900 yuan, respectively, also well below the pre-sale price.

Recent findings suggest that all versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade LFP Batteries. RWD models use a single 402 hp (300kW) electric motor, delivering CLTC ranges of 453 miles (730 km) for the base Premium model and 528 miles (850 km) for the Laser Premium and Laser Flagship versions.

Upgrading to the dual-motor AWD powertrain bumps power to 690 hp (515 kW) and delivers a CLTC range of up to 478 miles (770 km).

The optional AWD steer-by-wire package adds a premium touch with a drive-by-wire digital chassis, reclining driver’s seats, a 35.4″ integrated Star Ring display screen, and intelligent electric all-wheel-drive.

All versions feature BYD’s Flash Charging tech, enabling it to charge from 10% to 80% in five minutes, or nine minutes for a full recharge (10% to 97%).

Inside, the flagship SUV adopts a five-seat layout and is packed with huge digital screens and premium extras.

The third-gen Tang features two giant screens: a 35.4″ integrated Star Ring display and a 30″ panoramic theater screen.

It has been revealed that BYD said the five-seat setup opens up interior space for passengers, claiming the fresh Tang SUV has the largest front trunk (frunk) in its class at 205L. It also offers a generous 1,000 mm of legroom for rear passengers.

The flagship electric SUV is equipped with BYD’s latest tech and other features, including its God’s Eye B laser-assisted driving system with DiPilot300 and Disus-A dual-chamber intelligent air suspension body control system.

BYD’s God’s Eye B uses a roof-mounted LiDAR to support ADAS features such as city navigation assist, high-speed navigation assist, and all-scenario parking assist.

The third-gen Tang also has BYD’s newly introduced high-speed tire blowout stability system, which can keep the vehicle stable and in its lane at up to 112 mph (180 km/h).

Measuring 5,045 mm long, 1,980 mm wide, and 1,760 mm tall, with a 2,950 mm wheelbase, BYD’s newly introduced Tang SUV is about the size of a Tesla Model X or BMW iX.

The third-gen Tang will join the larger Great Tang as BYD expands its flagship SUV lineup. The Great Tang received over 150,000 preorders by the time it rolled out in mid-June, a record for a single BYD model.

Since it launched, BYD has sold over 10,000 Great Tangs a month for four consecutive months. Will the smaller five-seat Tang draw the same demand? Let us know what you think of it in the comments below.

The new facility in Debrecen, the first one that started churning out Neue Klasse-based EVs, went down in history for the fastest production ramp of any new BMW Group factory, with just eight months needed to achieve mass production at a sustained pace.

BMW iX4 production in Debrecen, Hungary.

The second and third shifts were added ahead of schedule to keep up with the higher-than-expected demand for the iX3, and the plant has been running around the clock since September. Since early November, the factory has added the iX4 to its lineup, boosting its output even further.

The fresh i3, which has nothing in common with the quirky first-generation electric hatchback, has seen high demand, prompting the automaker to open the order books in Europe earlier than originally planned. What’s more, the historic plant in Munich that has made gas-powered cars for all of its existence has been converted to build EVs, marking a big shift right at the heart of the Bavarian manufacturer.

Separately, the upcoming iX5, which is not based on the Neue Klasse architecture but borrows a lot of tech from the new platform, has started rolling off the line in Spartanburg, South Carolina, marking the beginning of EV manufacturing in the United States for BMW.

Recent findings suggest that getting back to the iX4, the start of production means that the first customers should start receiving their cars sooner rather than later, including those in the U.S. In fact, U.S.-spec iX4s are among the first to roll off the line in Hungary. Based on the same underpinnings as the massively successful iX3, the coupe-like EV boasts an EPA-estimated range of 428 miles and a dual-motor powertrain that develops a combined 463 horsepower.

The 112.2-kilowatt-hour battery can be charged from a DC stall at up to 400 kilowatts, with a 10-minute session resulting in up to 183 miles of range added, which is just one mile short compared to the technically similar iX3 50 xDrive. On AC power, the iX4 can accept up to 15.4 kW.

The 2027 BMW iX4 50 xDrive, the only one that’s on sale right now, starts at $66,200 plus destination.

#132579. Why Couldn’t I Be Happy for Someone I Love?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Why Couldn’t I Be Happy for Someone I Love?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.
  • This article was written in collaboration with Anna Goldfarb, author of Modern Friendship.
  • In a recent development, with the holidays upon us, many of us will gather with loved ones, sharing platefuls of food, laughter, and crucial updates about our lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.

This article was written in collaboration with Anna Goldfarb, author of Modern Friendship.

In a recent development, with the holidays upon us, many of us will gather with loved ones, sharing platefuls of food, laughter, and crucial updates about our lives. If you’re recently engaged, expecting, or have received an impressive accolade at work, what better time to announce the news than when you’re all in the same room?

But hearing someone’s good news can be unexpectedly fraught, especially if you’re struggling. You might want to rejoice for them but find you can’t. By understanding why good news is uniquely powerful in making or breaking a relationship, you can navigate the holidays with self-compassion and avoid a sting from swelling into something bigger.

Sources indicate that when we receive a friend’s bad news, we learn where we stand in their life. Finding out about our friend’s surgery through the grapevine, for example, reveals something about the closeness of the bond: the earlier we’re told, the closer we feel to that friend.

If you find out you’re not in their inner circle of confidantes, it can make you question how close your friendship even was: “Fluffy died, and you didn’t tell me? Am I even your best friend?”.

Good news reveals closeness too. Researchers call it a norm of close friendship to share good news, so when we don’t, our friends may question how close we are. When we hide good news from others, research finds, they report feeling more insulted and less close to us.

Hearing that a dear friend is engaged, expecting, or has scored a promotion reshapes how we think about our own experience. While we may have felt at peace with our job title, hearing that a friend got promoted may make us suddenly feel inadequate. We compare our friend’s newly achieved status to our own, and make inferences regarding our value. Good news, then, forces us to confront our status.

Of course, this doesn’t happen all the time. If someone else’s positive news is in an area you don’t identify with, you can revel in their success. Your friend can win an award for being the best baker in the tri-state area. If you don’t care about being an elite baker, cheering them on doesn’t require you to measure yourself against them. However, if you also dream of being an accomplished baker, it will be much harder to be happy for them because of what their good news means for you.

It has been revealed that abraham Tesser’s Self-Evaluation Maintenance Model (1988) explains this well. His model predicts that when someone close to you outperforms you in an area central to who you are and what you care about, the comparison uniquely stings. That’s why we might take someone’s good news personally.

Here are two questions to help you figure out why you couldn’t be happy for someone when you wanted to be:.

Answers to the first question are usually:.

Each feeling points to a source.

Answers to the second question can reveal common closeness and status concerns:.

I wasn’t told when I expected to be.

I felt unimportant to my friend.

I wasn’t sure what it meant for me moving forward.

I felt less content with my own life.

It has been revealed that sometimes the answer is simpler: I wanted it for myself. That’s envy, and it’s normal.

Recent findings suggest that as you hear happy updates from others this holiday season, be gentle with yourself, as you might’ve just learned something fresh about your relationship with the other person. It’s normal to have complicated feelings in the moment.

If you felt excluded because you weren’t told when you expected to be, start by celebrating their news, if you can. Later, you can let them know you’d love to hear updates sooner: “I love hearing your news. I hope you know you can always come to me with things like this.” Opening the conversation this way will hopefully give you more insight into their thinking. It also helps to reflect on who heard first and why. Do those people play a bigger role in your friend’s life right now? Are there sensible reasons your friend told other people first? Perhaps this friend shares work updates with you, but keeps personal updates to another circle. Now you know how they regard your relationship, and you can recalibrate your expectations.

If you felt inadequate after hearing the news, you’ll probably need some time and space to process the jolt. For example, if your friend is having a baby and you’ve recently had a miscarriage, you can tell your friend, “I’m so happy for you, and I need a little time to take it in. I’ll call you this weekend.” If you simply wanted the thing for yourself, own it: I wanted that job. Envy points to something you want, and you can still show up warmly while the envious feeling settles.

By understanding why you’re struggling to be happy for people you love, you give yourself the best chance of keeping the relationship once the feelings pass.

U.S. Loses Measles-Free Status After 26 Years, a Major Public Health Setback

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1341 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, a major public health achievement that was secured 26 years ago.
  • It has been revealed that the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the World Health Organization’s (WHO) regional office for the Americas, determined that measles has spread continuously in the U.S.
  • In a recent development, “Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” PAHO’s director, Jarbas Barbosa, MD, MPH, PhD, mentioned in a media briefing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, a major public health achievement that was secured 26 years ago.

It has been revealed that the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the World Health Organization’s (WHO) regional office for the Americas, determined that measles has spread continuously in the U.S. for more than 12 months. On November 17, PAHO unveiled the end of the country’s measles elimination status, which it has held since 2000.

In a recent development, “Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” PAHO’s director, Jarbas Barbosa, MD, MPH, PhD, mentioned in a media briefing. “It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at risk of a preventable illness, hospitalization, and death.”.

PAHO’s review examined measles spread starting January 20, 2025, when the first person became ill in a large West Texas outbreak, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

It has been revealed that CDC data show 5,412 confirmed measles cases this year as of November 12. That’s the highest annual total since 1991 and more than double the 2025 count of 2,289 cases.

Recent findings suggest that andi Shane, MD, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta, called the U.S. losing measles elimination status “a public health alarm that we are not being effective and we’re not controlling measles as well.”.

The measles virus is highly contagious. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. People can catch it in a room up to two hours after an infected person has left, according to the CDC.

“There’s really been very little measles in the United States over the past 25 years until January 2025,” William Moss, MD, a professor of epidemiology at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, told Healthline.

Losing the status itself doesn’t change much about daily life for most Americans, Moss stated. The concern is the measles outbreaks, hospitalizations and deaths behind the loss, he said.

He called the loss “a big red flag” after “enormous efforts over the past 26 years” to keep the status.

Recent findings suggest that A country loses its elimination status when there is “uninterrupted circulation of the same virus genotype and lineage for 12 months or more,” according to PAHO. Shane explained it this way: “For the past 12 months in the United States, we’ve had ongoing circulation of the measles virus and person-to-person transmission is occurring.”.

According to recent reports, canada lost its elimination status in November 2025, and the U.K. and five European countries lost theirs earlier in 2026.

The U.S. can regain the status. “Other countries have done that,” Moss noted. Brazil, which lost its status in 2019, regained it in November 2024. Venezuela, which lost its status in 2018, regained it in 2023, according to PAHO.

Industry observers note that before the measles vaccine, measles infected an estimated 3 million to 4 million Americans each year, according to the CDC. Among reported cases, about 400 to 500 people died each year, 48,000 needed hospital care, and 1,000 developed encephalitis, or brain swelling.

Here’s a timeline of measles elimination in the U.S.:.

Moss said elimination efforts “really intensified” after a large outbreak from 1989 to 1992. Part of that push was “really promoting school entry vaccination checks,” he said.

“That was one of the key policy changes that I think allowed for measles elimination in the United States.”.

Every state and Washington, D.C., require children to be vaccinated against measles to attend school, though exemptions vary by state, according to the nonprofit health policy organization KFF.

Fewer kindergartners are getting the MMR vaccine, according to the CDC.

According to recent reports, kindergarten MMR coverage fell from 95.2% in the 2019–2020 school year to 92.4% in 2025–2026. About 280,000 kindergartners started the 2025–2026 school year without records showing they had completed the MMR series, the CDC reported.

Shane remarked “95 out of 100 people need to be protected against measles” for a community to get herd protection.

“So since we’ve been below that for many, many months, that is also contributing to the loss of our elimination status,” she remarked.

In a recent development, “It takes two things to have a measles outbreak,” Moss said. A community needs low vaccine coverage, and someone with measles has to enter it and “start the chain of transmission,” he said.

About 96% of this year’s cases were among people who were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status, up from 93% in 2025, according to the CDC.

Moss mentioned many of those cases are adults.

“This is particularly true in Pennsylvania, where about two-thirds of the cases are in adults,” he mentioned. Many never got vaccinated as kids and grew up while measles was rare, so they never built natural immunity, he said.

He noted that having so many unvaccinated adults puts pregnant people and adults with chronic conditions like lung disease at risk of serious illness. The U.S. has already seen “dozens of pregnant women actually getting infected during pregnancy,” he said.Infected parents can also spread measles to young children and grandparents, Shane said. Shane traced much of the hesitancy to the pandemic. “With COVID there’s been an overall distrust in vaccines and vaccination that initially started with COVID but has now spread to other vaccines,” she said.

Sources indicate that moss pointed to the federal government. “We know what it takes to achieve and sustain elimination. We have the expertise. We have the resources,” he stated.

He cited staff cuts at the CDC and said messaging from Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and President Donald Trump has undermined vaccine confidence. He called federal messaging on vaccines “really mixed and weak.”.

Moss also criticized the President’s August 10 executive order calling for the MMR vaccine to be split into separate shots for each disease.

“There’s no justification for that, and those vaccines don’t even exist in the United States,” he said.

Industry observers note that measles may cause ear infections, diarrhea, pneumonia, encephalitis and, in some cases, death, according to the CDC. The disease may also weaken the immune system for weeks to a year after recovery, raising the risk of flu, COVID-19, or RSV, Shane said. “It’s not a benign childhood disease,” Moss said.

It has been revealed that the best protection against measles is two doses of the MMR vaccine, which are about 97% effective, according to the CDC. Shane noted, “There are not very many other things we do in life that give you such great protection.” People who missed doses can still catch up, she added. “If you just don’t know or can’t tell, there’s no harm — as long as you’re eligible — in getting another MMR vaccine.”.

Shane added that “parents really want to do the right thing for their children.”.

“We know that the MMR vaccine — that’s the vaccine that provides protection against measles — is a safe vaccine. It’s a very effective vaccine,” Shane said.

Babies under 12 months are too young for the vaccine. “So they depend on the protection of the people around them,” Shane mentioned.

Sources indicate that the CDC recommends a first MMR dose at 12 to 15 months and a second at 4 to 6 years. Babies 6 to 11 months old who will travel internationally should get an early dose, and adults without proof of immunity should get at least one dose, according to the CDC.

To stop the outbreaks, Moss said the U.S. will need to “increase vaccine coverage, particularly in those communities that have had long-standing low vaccine rates.”.

Sources indicate that so far, the response has been “more reactive than proactive,” Moss said. Public health teams scramble once an outbreak starts, he said, and he wants more outreach to at-risk communities before measles arrives.

“I am worried about the ability of the United States to regain measles elimination status in the current climate,” Moss remarked.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for as long as humans have looked at the night sky, we’ve wondered what lies beyond Earth—and dreamed up ways of getting up there. These days, powerful rockets carrying tons of fuel are the tried-and-true method of escaping the planet’s gravitational pull and reaching space.

Sources indicate that but what if, instead of modern rockets, we went medieval? Could a trebuchet or catapult—the massive siege weapons once used to fling stones at castles—launch a person into orbit? And if so, just how big would one have to be?

The answer requires a little imagination, a lot of physics, and a space-launching siege weapon of truly ridiculous proportions.

According to recent reports, A catapult is essentially a giant lever used to hurl projectiles. Typically, they have a large, spoon-shaped throwing arm that’s wrenched back, creating tension, and then released, flinging an object over a great distance.

A trebuchet is a kind of catapult that uses a counterweight and gravity to launch projectiles. This machine’s long arm rests on a fulcrum, with a sling or cup for the projectile at one end and a heavy counterweight at the other.

When the arm is released, gravity pulls the counterweight downward, sending the opposite end—and its payload—soaring upward and forward.

According to recent reports, trebuchets are typically more powerful than catapults because they can launch heavier payloads over greater distances. So for our purposes, we’ll be focusing on a space trebuchet rather than a space catapult.

Trebuchets have been hurling heavy objects through the air for centuries. The structures are believed to have originated in China as early as the fifth century BC and eventually spread across Eurasia, becoming a formidable force in medieval warfare.

They arrived in Europe during the 12th century and swiftly surpassed simple catapults.

According to recent reports, today, trebuchets are no longer used as weapons. But they remain popular as teaching tools for demonstrating physics principles—and for the decidedly more wholesome pursuit of seeing how far we can fling pumpkins, cabbages, and other projectiles.

So let’s crunch the numbers: Could a massive trebuchet really blast a human into orbit? Theoretically, yes. Practically, no.

Sources indicate that for help answering this question, Popular Science turned to Frankie Zhu, an assistant professor in space robotics at the Colorado School of Mines in Golden, Colorado. Zhu gamely agreed to do some back-of-the-napkin math to put some numbers to this wildly improbable scenario.

“It just reminds me of a classic physics problem you would encounter in undergrad,” she says.

Before we can get to the heart of the calculations, Zhu says, we need to define some initial parameters. First, because the energy required to send a human into orbit depends on both mass and velocity, we need to know our imaginary astronaut’s mass. Zhu recommends 70 kilograms, or about 154 pounds.

Next, we need to define where space—and, for our purposes, orbit—begins. The conventional boundary is the Kármán line, an imaginary line 100 kilometers (about 62 miles) above sea level that is widely used to mark the edge of space. It’s the point at which Earth’s atmosphere becomes too thin for conventional aircraft to generate enough lift to stay aloft. “An orbit at 100 kilometers would be the lowest energy orbit possible,” she says.

To orbit Earth at the Kármán line—and not plummet back to the ground—a person needs to travel at approximately 7.85 kilometers per second, or 17,500 miles per hour, the same speed the International Space Station travels while orbiting Earth. “Any less and the human would fly up and then come back down in a parabolic trajectory,” she notes.

If we assume that the atmosphere doesn’t produce drag on the human as they fly, then the velocity of the person leaving the trebuchet immediately after launch needs to be at least 7.97 kilometers per second, or 17,828 miles per hour. That extra bit of speed accounts for the energy needed to climb from Earth’s surface to the Kármán line.

In a recent development, to launch a human at that velocity, the trebuchet would need to store a massive amount of potential energy—about 2.22 billion joules, by Zhu’s calculations, similar to about 1,200 pounds of TNT. Zhu notes that she’s assuming 100 percent mechanical efficiency, meaning that none of the trebuchet’s stored energy is lost to friction, air resistance, sound, deformation, or the movement of the machine itself.

According to recent reports, from here, we can move on to the design of the trebuchet. Based on Zhu’s math, the trebuchet would need a 5,000-ton counterweight—the equivalent of roughly 950 African bush elephants—which would need to drop at least 45.2 meters, or roughly 148 feet.

To turn the relatively slow movement of the massive counterweight into a hypersonic launch speed, the trebuchet would need an extreme mechanical leverage ratio of 379:1, she says. With these figures in mind, the trebuchet’s long throwing arm—the part with the human at the end of it—would need to be about 17.14 kilometers, or 10.7 miles, long.

“That should give you all the physical parameters of the trebuchet, ignoring some physics and human welfare,” she jokes.

It has been revealed that how exactly would a human fare under these conditions? Fighter jet pilots can survive up to nine Gs using specialized G-suits, physical straining techniques, and intense centrifuge training. But, Zhu claims, the “amount of Gs that the trebuchet is going to reach is…definitely past nine Gs. This human is not going to be alive when they make it to orbit.”.

Another hurdle? Building the trebuchet. “To design a structure that can handle that amount of mass—the 5,000-ton counterweight—to support that mass and then to make something that large… that would be a humanity feat and a structural feat,” she says.

According to recent reports, how much trash is on the moon? About 412,000 pounds.

Why can’t we just launch all of Earth’s garbage into the sun?

What happens to your body when you die in space?

Is turbulence really like Jell-O? Pilots weigh in.

According to recent reports, why do we put seatbacks up for landing? An aviation expert explains.

It has been revealed that A more human-friendly option, she states, might be a railgun, which uses electromagnetic forces to accelerate a projectile along a pair of conductive rails at extremely high speeds. To launch a person into orbit, a railgun would also need to be “really, really long,” she says. But because the human projectile could accelerate over a much greater distance and for a longer period of time, a railgun would theoretically offer a smoother acceleration profile—one that’s more amenable to human survival.

“Whereas [with] a trebuchet, the acceleration is going to be impulsive,” she says. “It’s going to be a huge smack at the very beginning if the structure doesn’t flex, if the structure is rigid.”.

Rockets have been the standard for launching things into space since 1944, when Germany’s V-2 became the first human-made object to cross the Kármán line. But that doesn’t necessarily mean they’re the most efficient way to get there.

Rockets require enormous amounts of fuel, and all of that propellant has to be carried onboard. In other words, a rocket has to spend fuel lifting not just its payload, but also the fuel it needs to keep accelerating. This makes getting off Earth an inherently energy-intensive—and expensive—proposition.

Sources indicate that with that in mind, engineers continue to explore other ways of getting into space, ideally using less fuel and resources. So far, though, most of their ideas haven’t made it off the drawing board—and, after crunching the numbers, Zhu says it’s highly unlikely that trebuchets will ever replace rockets.

“A lot of ideas are fantastical, some are possible, and an even smaller set are economical,” notes Zhu.

Industry News: Here’s How the Porsche 718 Boxster EV’s Fake Flat-Six and PDK Work

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the upcoming Porsche 718 Boxster EV hops on board the growing simulated-internal-combustion-engine-and-transmission electric car trend.
  • Industry observers note that the system that debuted in the Taycan is still called “E-Shift” here in the Boxster, and you can turn it on or off via a button on the steering wheel.
  • “It was a massive discussion in our tech giant,” Lefevre said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the upcoming Porsche 718 Boxster EV hops on board the growing simulated-internal-combustion-engine-and-transmission electric car trend. We just drove a prototype, and while there’s a lot to discuss about the car in general, it’s also worth honing in on the sound aspect. As you might expect, it’s rather pivotal to the experience behind the wheel.

Industry observers note that the system that debuted in the Taycan is still called “E-Shift” here in the Boxster, and you can turn it on or off via a button on the steering wheel. Porsche chose the 3.4-liter naturally aspirated flat-six from the 981-generation Boxster as its muse. It’s a good choice, but also a bit of a surprise considering the spectacular sound out of the 4.0-liter flat-six found in the previous 718 Boxsters. But Porsche has its reasons, as Dr.-Ing. Sebastian Lefevre, team lead advanced driver assistance systems 718, tells us.

“It was a massive discussion in our tech giant,” Lefevre said. “From our point of view, the 4.0 engine is a little bit too soft in the sound. In our company, the 981 GTS sound, six-cylinder, was a little bit louder, and it would also feel more popular and familiar with our old customers.”.

Once you hear the sound, there’s a good chance you’ll end up agreeing with Porsche. Lefevre mentioned the possibility of using the four-cylinder from the previous 718, but just as quickly shot the idea down referencing critique of the flat-four’s sound. How it reproduced the engine and exhaust via speakers is similar to how other OEMs with simulated internal combustion engines in EVs do it.

“A lot of microphones outside, inside,” Lefevre said. “And then we measured it all over the complete rpm range. And then we put it here, in this car, and measure it again. With the speakers, which are installed here. We have two.”.

The most controversial speaker is bound to be the exterior-positioned one. More than anything, however, this exterior speaker exists as a sound maker for occupants to enjoy when the roof is off. It tries to emulate a mid-engine powertrain arrangement by way of the sound emanating from behind the driver and passenger; Porsche increases the volume inside the car with the roof removed, too. That’s a neat idea, but one that struggles to work in practice; I could hear some faint backfires on “downshifts” like Porsche’s ICE cars produce, but the experience is far from that of a real exhaust and engine echoing and reverberating off mountainsides or buildings.

Recent findings suggest that mercedes-AMG has the best ICE simulation around right now, with its AMG GT 4-Door Coupe going so far as to induce proper NVH characteristics by using exciters in the seats. The Boxster EV Prototype we drove relies entirely on the speakers to induce its hypnosis. But E-Shift brings a few theatrics to the table.

According to recent reports, when lining up for a launch control start, Porsche pulses the torque of the electric motor to give a sense of an impending launch. It also lets you run the car into “redline,” tossing you forward with brake torque, just as it would in a manually-shifted gas-powered car. That mentioned, Porsche took some liberties with the 8000-rpm redline depicted in this prototype; the 981 Boxster GTS instrument cluster shows a redline of 7600 rpm, so you have an extra 400 fake revs to play with in the EV.

Industry observers note that not as though this extra headroom matters, however, as Porsche chose to not simulate the torque curve of the flat-six. Instead, peak performance from the single electric motor is always available, and the car shuffles through its fake seven gears as speeds rise and fall. How it shifts is dependent on drive mode per usual with Porsche PDKs, and you can choose between manual or automatic shifting. You’ll even hear a tone difference in the engine noise over the speakers depending on whether you’re on- or off-throttle, just as you would were the real 3.4-liter be gulping in air behind your head.

For our full first impressions from behind the wheel of the 718 Boxster EV, make sure you read our prototype drive review.

The Bayern and Werder Bremen legend Claudio Pizarro is famously the Bundesliga’s oldest ever player, after turning out well past 40 years of age - up front no less. But he’s making an appearance in FC 26 because he won the Hero Vote Poll a few months ago, with the Peruvian edging out notable nutter Steffan Effenberg and the prolific Brazilian striker, Elber.

The love for South American Heroes continues with Ivan Zamorano presented in his Real Madrid guise rather than part of the unbelievably stacked Inter squad which featured legends and Icons ranging from current Atletico Madrid manager Diego Simeone to Javier Zanetti and Ronaldo Nazario.

And probably most interestingly, Queen of the Jungle and centurion Lioness, Jill Scott, is also coming to shore up the midfield with a card which fits the “Gullit Gang” pre-requisite of all face stats over 80 - including a dominant 91 physical befitting her role as one of the most recognisable enforcers in women’s football.

Whether her in-game body type will actually let her put that strength out on the pitch (she will surely also have Bruiser) remains to be seen, but she could easily have the gangly aura of Patrick Vieira if the rest of her PlayStyles are right.

New Ultimate Team Heroes have been added mid-season before, including the likes of Enzo Francescoli in FC 24, but 3 at once looks to indicate that EA is leaning on Heroes to add fan-favourite players to the game with a lower threshold than Icons.

Plus they can be given away for free without upsetting the power curve as much as Icons, as shown by the free Classic XI Heroes handed out recently (I got Mario Gomez, F).

The rest of the Winter Wildcards team features a host of equally famous, and now infamous, players with some featuring 99 stats and alternative positions.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Trump claims he “protected” Elon Musk during his first term, and that “you wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me.” He tied it to “a certain incident” that he called “a tough incident,” but he didn’t say what it was.
  • Musk had plenty of run-ins with federal regulators between 2017 and 2021.
  • Trump called in to CNBC’s Squawk on the Street on Monday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Trump claims he “protected” Elon Musk during his first term, and that “you wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me.” He tied it to “a certain incident” that he called “a tough incident,” but he didn’t say what it was.

Musk had plenty of run-ins with federal regulators between 2017 and 2021. One of them could have ended his career as a public tech giant CEO, and it’s our best guess.

Trump called in to CNBC’s Squawk on the Street on Monday. That same morning, Nvidia’s board voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, and in its press release it said it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government” before concluding Huang posed no national security risk.

Trump argued that the US needs to “protect our geniuses.” Then he brought up Musk:.

Industry observers note that “You know, I protected Elon in my first term. Very big. Elon was protected. I talk about it, and I’m proud of Elon. I love Elon. I think he’s great. You know, 80% super genius, 20% he has other problems. But I tell him that. But Elon, I protected. You wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me. And, you know, a certain incident took place, which was, you know, a tough incident.”.

Sources indicate that it’s not the first time he has hinted at it. Last week, in a Fox News interview from Shenzhen, Trump said: “I helped Elon a lot in my first term. I helped him a lot. He was in big trouble.” Back in 2024, he told CNBC he had helped Musk “when I was president,” again without details.

Sources indicate that on August 7, 2018, Musk tweeted that he was “considering taking Tesla private at $420. Funding secured.” It wasn’t. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund had shown interest, but no deal or price had been agreed, and the take-private plan was dead within three weeks.

Industry observers note that the SEC sued Musk for securities fraud on September 27, 2018. The agency didn’t only ask for a fine. It asked the court to bar Musk from serving as an officer or director of any public tech giant. That would have meant no more Elon at Tesla, which lines up with “you wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me” better than anything else on this list.

Industry observers note that and then it went away fast. Two days later, the SEC declared a settlement: Musk stayed CEO, gave up the chairman title for three years, and he and Tesla each paid $20 million, $40 million in total. Tesla added two independent directors and agreed to have a lawyer pre-approve Musk’s material tweets, but the SEC never fully enforced it. Musk didn’t admit or deny anything.

The SEC was run at the time by Jay Clayton, a Trump appointee.

There was a criminal side too. In September 2018, federal prosecutors in San Francisco opened a fraud investigation over the same tweet. It never led to charges, and the Justice Department never said publicly why.

The SEC came back in February 2019 and asked a judge to hold Musk in contempt after he tweeted Tesla production guidance without pre-approval. That one ended in April with an amended deal listing the topics he needed approval for, and no latest penalty.

In May 2020, Musk reopened the Fremont factory in defiance of Alameda County’s COVID orders and tweeted: “If anyone is arrested, I ask that it only be me.” Trump tweeted the next day that California “should let Tesla & @elonmusk open the plant, NOW.” But the county was already working toward a reopening date of May 18, and a president doesn’t control county health orders.

In a recent development, there’s also the September 2018 Joe Rogan episode, where Musk smoked a joint on camera. NASA followed with a workplace safety review of SpaceX and Boeing, and SpaceX lives on federal contracts.

For context, Musk sat on Trump’s business advisory councils early in that first term, and quit in June 2017 when Trump pulled out of the Paris Agreement. That feels like a lifetime ago now that xAI runs its data centers on natural gas turbines.

Our money is on “funding secured.”.

It has been revealed that musk revealed a take-private deal at a specific price that the other side never agreed to, and the stock jumped. It’s textbook securities fraud. The main remedy was supposed to be independent oversight. Tesla gave the chair to Robyn Denholm, who had been on the board since 2014, and the board has done what Musk wanted ever since: it defended his pay packages, approved new ones, and stayed quiet while the brand took damage. The Cybertruck almost certainly does not happen, at least not in its current form. Instead, they would have developed a more conventional pickup. We'd have gotten 2nd generation models of the X and S instead of them being canceled. Instead of a Cybercab, there would be a model 2 compact car people could buy. And there would likely be a Tesla van and a full sized SUV, possibly developed on the same underlying platform. Also, the SEC was trying to ban him from running public companies. At the time, SpaceX was still private. So, Elon could have still run SpaceX.

Trump likes to take credit, and he could be inflating his role here. But if the White House leaned on the SEC or the Justice Department in 2018 to help a CEO facing fraud allegations, that’s a serious problem, and someone should look into it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the 2027 Cadillac Vistiq just got a little more expensive, as spotted by GM Authority. For the latest iteration of the relatively young three-row electric SUV that slots under the huge Escalade IQ, Cadillac wants between $900 and $1,000 more than a month ago.

The higher starting price doesn’t necessarily mean more equipment, though the Vistiq now comes with a native Tesla-style NACS charging port, just like all the other 2027 EVs made by General Motors.

That said, the automaker is not throwing in any complimentary adapters, so owners who want a manufacturer-approved DC fast-charging adapter to use at CCS stalls will have to shell out an extra $189, even if they opt for the top-spec Platinum trim that starts at roughly $100,000.

For what it’s worth, Cadillac is offering a charging adapter bundle that includes a CCS1 adapter and an AC adapter for J1772 stations for a total of $256, which is quite good value for money.

Compared to the 2026 Vistiq, the 2027 model brings two fresh optional appearance packages and a few new exterior paint colors. The Onyx Package, which is only available on the top Platinum trim, comes with 23-inch black wheels, gloss black nameplates, Obsidian Chrome mirror caps, and puddle lamps that depict the Cadillac logo. Then, there’s the Onyx Lite package, which can be had on the Sport trim only. It features all of the goodies in the big Onyx pack, except the 23-inch wheels.

As standard, the 2027 Cadillac Vistiq comes with 21-inch Bright Silver alloy wheels, a dual-motor powertrain capable of outputting 615 horsepower and 650 pound-feet of torque, and a 102-kilowatt-hour battery that enables a maximum EPA-estimated range of 305 miles.

Industry observers note that the Luxury and Sport trims come standard with an 11.5-kW on-board charger, while the Premium Luxury and Platinum trims come standard with an upgraded on-board charger capable of accepting up to 19.2 kW from a Level 2 dispenser. The uprated on-board charger can be spec’d on the first two trims, too, but it costs an additional $1,480.

For 2027, the Luxury and Premium Luxury trims cost $900 more than the outgoing model, while the Sport and Platinum trims are now $1,000 more expensive than before. As a result, the 2027 Cadillac Vistiq now starts at $80,395, while the top trim’s MSRP is now $99,495.

All trims get the same powertrain, but the more expensive versions come with more kit as standard.

Sources indicate that the Home Depot’s 2026 Black Friday sale has 65 power tool and accessory deals worth a look, led by $99 brushless kits and battery starter packs that include a free bare tool. You can browse the full Black Friday tool sale, or jump straight to the lists below, grouped by free-tool promo, brand and category.

It has been revealed that two rules make this sale easier to navigate. First, buying a $99 to $199 battery starter kit with a free tool often costs the same as—or less than—buying that bare tool on its own. Second, watch out for decoy discounts on older brushed drills and mixed bundles that sit right next to newer brushless kits (brushless motors run cooler, last longer and stretch battery runtime). We checked prices and stock at The Home Depot on Wednesday, Nov. 25, ahead of Thanksgiving and Black Friday; pricing and free-tool options can vary by store.

A drill, an impact driver and two batteries for $169.

Sources indicate that A drill/driver and an impact driver cover most of what a homeowner asks of cordless tools, and the DeWalt Atomic 20V Max 2-tool combo kit cuts $80 off a compact entry into DeWalt’s battery system. The bag packs the DCD794 drill/driver, the DCF809 impact driver, two 2.0Ah batteries and a charger—a practical baseline if you’re comparing the best tool combo kits. The brushless impact driver is rated at 1,700 inch-pounds of torque, while the drill’s 5.88-inch head slips easily inside cabinets. Both batteries fit the rest of DeWalt’s 20V Max lineup.

Half off a brushless Milwaukee drill with a battery.

At $99, the Milwaukee M18 brushless 1/2-inch compact drill/driver kit is the cheapest clean on-ramp into Milwaukee’s M18 battery platform. Measuring 5.7 inches front to back, it fits inside cabinets and between joists without forcing awkward angles. Milwaukee rates the motor at 550 inch-pounds of torque and up to 1,700 rpm, and the box includes one 2.0Ah battery, a charger and a soft bag. If you drive more lag bolts and deck screws than you drill holes, grab the matching M18 compact brushless impact driver kit for the same $99 (or check our picks for the best impact drivers).

Two 4.0Ah batteries, a charger and a free tool.

In a recent development, buy the batteries and the tool comes free. The Ridgid 18V Max Output starter kit pairs two 4.0Ah packs and a charger for $149, and The Home Depot discounts one eligible item in your cart to $0. Standouts on the eight-item menu include a brushless 6-1/2-inch circular saw, a mid-torque impact wrench, an angle grinder, a jigsaw and a 6.0Ah battery. Don’t skip the paperwork after delivery: Ridgid’s Lifetime Service Agreement covers free parts and service on eligible tools bought at The Home Depot, but only if you register them and upload proof of purchase within 90 days.

Level lines across a room for under $50.

Hanging a gallery wall or a run of cabinets goes faster with a plumb line already projected across the room. Down to $49.97 from $95, the Bosch GLL50-20 self-leveling cross-line laser casts red horizontal and vertical lines rated out to 50 feet, with an IP55 dust- and water-resistance rating. It runs on included AA batteries (Bosch sells a 3.7V rechargeable pack separately) and mounts via magnets or a 1/4-inch-20 thread (standard camera-tripod mount). Like most red-beam lasers, this model is built strictly for indoor work; step up to a pricier green-beam pick from our guide to the best laser levels if you work in bright, sunlit rooms.

Four other brands mirror the Ridgid starter kit above: add the qualifying battery or combo kit to your cart and select a free tool at checkout. The Ryobi ONE+ starter kit is the lowest buy-in at $99, while the $199 DeWalt 20V Max 6.0Ah and 4.0Ah starter kit unlocks 14 free options (check your ZIP code at checkout, as high-value bare tools sell out unevenly by store). A higher amp-hour (Ah) rating means longer runtime—2.0Ah packs keep drills light overhead, while 4.0Ah to 6.0Ah packs keep circular saws and grinders from bogging down.

Recent findings suggest that milwaukee’s 12V (M12) and 18V (M18) batteries don’t cross over, and anything labeled “tool only” ships without a battery or charger. Fuel marks Milwaukee’s flagship brushless tier, while Packout refers to its interlocking modular toolbox system. Note that the half-off M18 5-tool combo kit ($349) and 9-tool combo kit ($699) are not Fuel sets and mix in older brushed tools—fine for weekend projects, but check the box list if you want all-brushless gear. The M12 4.0Ah battery two-pack also drops to $79, and the $99 M18 drill kit sits near the top of this page.

Industry observers note that don’t scroll past the 20V Max brushless 3-speed oscillating multi-tool kit at $99—getting the tool, a charger and a 4.0Ah battery at half price is one of the quietest steals in this sale. Meanwhile, watch out for the two standalone drills: the $129 20V Max drill/driver kit throws in two tiny 1.3Ah packs, but its DCD771 uses an older brushed motor. Most shoppers are better off spending $30 less on the $99 Atomic compact drill/driver kit, which trades the spare battery for a shorter brushless tool and a higher-capacity 2.0Ah pack (or stepping up to the $169 Atomic 2-tool kit at the top of the page). For decoding DeWalt’s labels below: Atomic is its compact tier, XR is its pro-grade line and FlexVolt packs power both 20V and 60V tools.

Ryobi delivers the lowest kit prices in this roundup, though the cheapest drill deserves a caveat. The $49.97 ONE+ 3/8-inch drill/driver kit tops out at 600 rpm and lacks an adjustable clutch, making it easy to strip screws or overdrive fasteners. Spend $9 more on the ONE+ 1/2-inch drill/driver kit for a two-speed gearbox and real torque control. HP designates Ryobi’s brushless lineup, and if you already own a charger, the $99 4.0Ah battery two-pack is worth weighing against the $99 starter kit plus free tool listed earlier.

Skip the $149 two-battery starter kit if you only need one tool and a single pack: Ridgid’s $99 shelf includes a 4.0Ah battery with the 1/2-inch impact wrench kit, the 6-1/2-inch circular saw kit and the angle grinder kit.

According to recent reports, the headline benchtop cut is $200 off the DeWalt DWS780 12-inch sliding miter saw ($449), which uses an LED shadow-line cut indicator instead of a laser you have to recalibrate and tilts both left and right (double-bevel) so you don’t have to flip long trim boards. Note that the two pneumatic nailers below—the $99 DeWalt brad nailer and the $199 Makita AN924 framing nailer (which takes 21-degree plastic-collated nail strips)—require an air compressor and hose sold separately.

If you’re rounding out a latest drill or saw—or grabbing stocking stuffers—consumables start under $10 with the Ryobi 40-piece drill and impact drive kit at $9.97, and the Diablo framing blade two-pack is $12.88.

#132569. Upcoming Guidelines Recommend Routine Prostate Cancer Screening for Men Over 50

Upcoming Guidelines Recommend Routine Prostate Cancer Screening for Men Over 50

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1004 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As rates of advanced prostate cancer continue to rise, the American Cancer Society (ACS) has issued upcoming guidelines recommending routine prostate cancer screening for many men starting at age 50.
  • The updated recommendations, published November 12 in CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians, mark a shift from the organization’s previous emphasis on shared decision making about whether to undergo screening.
  • Under the upcoming guidelines, the ACS recommends regular prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing beginning at age 50 for men at average risk of prostate cancer and age 45 for those at higher risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As rates of advanced prostate cancer continue to rise, the American Cancer Society (ACS) has issued upcoming guidelines recommending routine prostate cancer screening for many men starting at age 50.

The updated recommendations, published November 12 in CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians, mark a shift from the organization’s previous emphasis on shared decision making about whether to undergo screening.

Under the upcoming guidelines, the ACS recommends regular prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing beginning at age 50 for men at average risk of prostate cancer and age 45 for those at higher risk.

Advances in MRI technology and biomarker testing may also help doctors determine which men need further testing, potentially reducing unnecessary biopsies and overtreatment.

The ACS last updated its prostate cancer screening guidelines in 2010, when conflicting research findings raised questions about whether the benefits of PSA screening outweighed the potential harms.

At the time, the organization emphasized informed, shared decision making between patients and healthcare professionals.

However, longer-term follow-up studies have since provided stronger evidence of the benefits of early detection, prompting the ACS to conduct a systematic review and enhancement its recommendations.

The authors of the report noted, “In making these recommendations, we recognize that PSA testing is only the first step in a screening cascade that includes secondary testing of men with an elevated PSA level and treatment decisions for men diagnosed with prostate cancer.”.

The fresh guidelines recommend a PSA test every 2 years for men ages 50–69 with an average risk of prostate cancer.

The recommendation for those at high risk is a PSA test every year starting at age 45.

Industry observers note that for men ages 70–74, the ACS recommends individualized decision making. If an individual chooses to be screened, the ACS recommends a PSA test every 2 years until the age of 74.

Ramkishen Narayanan, MD, Director of the Center for Urologic Health at The Roy and Patricia Disney Family Cancer Center at Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center in Burbank, CA, who wasn’t involved in the report, told Healthline that screening shouldn’t automatically be ruled out for men over 75.

“[A] point worth noting is that for men over 75, their PSA history as well as their individual clinical scenarios should be evaluated, and that PSA should not be discouraged in this group of men if their life expectancy and clinical history warrant a PSA check.”.

According to the ACS, approximately 1 in 8 men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer during their lifetime.

Individual risk depends on age, race/ethnicity, and other factors:.

Prostate cancer diagnoses in the United States increased by around 3% per year between 2014 and 2022, according to the ACS.

The rise in diagnoses, particularly advanced-stage prostate cancer, has renewed attention on the importance of regular screening.

Industry observers note that “[The] current state of prostate cancer screening guidelines is vague and generalized. This has led to ambiguity, disagreement, and variation of opinion among healthcare providers and institutions in their approach to men’s health,” mentioned S. Adam Ramin, MD, board certified urologist, urologic oncologist, and medical director of Urology Cancer Specialists in Los Angeles, CA, who wasn’t involved in the report.

The updated ACS guidelines drew partly on findings from a 2025 follow-up of the European Randomized Study of Screening for Prostate Cancer (ERSPC), which found that regular PSA screening was associated with a 13% reduction in prostate cancer deaths over 23 years.

A 12-year ERSPC follow-up in 2012 also suggested that regular screening was associated with a decrease in metastatic prostate cancer diagnosis, which is another finding that influenced the updated guidance.

“Prostate cancer can take many years, even decades, to become clinically significant, so it takes a long time for us to see the consequences of changes in screening practices,” Taylor Goodstein, MD, assistant professor of urology in the College of Medicine at the University of Cincinnati, who wasn’t involved in the report, told Healthline.

“With longer follow-up from randomized trials, we now have more convincing evidence that PSA screening reduces the risk of dying from prostate cancer,” she remarked.

“The ACS guidelines are vital now because they drive home the most important point that prostate cancer screening saves lives,” noted Narayanan.

Healthcare professionals use PSA levels to help determine whether additional testing for prostate cancer may be necessary.

The ACS recommends further testing for men under 70 with PSA levels of 3 ng/mL or higher.

According to recent reports, for those ages 70 and older, the ACS recommends further testing if their PSA is 6.5 ng/mL or higher. This is because PSA levels tend to be naturally higher in older men.

You can speak with your healthcare professional to find out more about PSA cutoff levels.

Goodstein told Healthline that the ways this fresh guidance can change the outlook for prostate cancer are simple.

“If we screen men, we can catch troublesome cancers early, before they have a chance to spread,” she stated.

Goodstein also emphasized how much the evaluation process has changed. In the past, an elevated PSA level often led directly to a biopsy.

Recent findings suggest that today, doctors generally repeat the PSA test within two weeks to three months to confirm the result. If PSA levels remain elevated, additional testing, including a prostate MRI or validated biomarker test, can help determine whether a biopsy is necessary.

Narayanan told Healthline, “The newly introduced guidelines will hopefully remove any confusion about the value of PSA screening and encourage prostate cancer screening as an integral part of a man’s ‘checkup’.”.

He added that it is worth noting that the DRE (digital rectal exam) adds little value to the initial prostate cancer screening and is no longer something that men should fear.

Recent findings suggest that “Adoption of this set of specific guidelines standardizes the approach to screening for prostate cancer. It provides a unified effort among all levels of healthcare. It most likely will increase the chances of finding prostate cancer in earlier stages and lead to improved cancer treatment outcomes,” mentioned Ramin.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eight years after a harrowing crash at Pocono Raceway paralyzed the then-IndyCar star, Robert Wickens has made his way to the grid of the biggest sports car race in the United States. He will contest the 2027 installment of the 24 Hours of Daytona in a Hanley Motorsports Inc.-run BMW M4 GT3, part of his first-ever full season of IMSA racing.

Industry observers note that wickens will pair with Mason Filippi in a full-season effort in the GTD class. Both drivers are champions in the IMSA Pilot Challenge TCR class; Wickens won the title in 2023, while Filippi scored his own championship in 2026. The pairing reunites two drivers that shared a DXDT Racing Corvette during the sprint races last season, the second such schedule for Wickens in the past two years. Their 2026 season was briefly interrupted when the team’s hauler caught fire on its way to the round at Laguna Seca.

Since those were all sprint races, Wickens would only have to get into or out of the car one time per race event. Endurance races are a latest challenge, one that will mean more driver changes complicated by his paralysis. It will also mean more chances to win, and opportunities to win his class in the country’s oldest and most prestigious sports car events. That opportunity is an exciting one, the biggest step yet what Wickens hopes is a long road back to the top.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve worked incredibly hard for a long time to reach this point in my career,” Wickens says, “and I’m filled with gratitude for everyone who has helped me achieve my goal of returning to the highest levels of motorsports... I couldn’t be more excited to get to work and compete in my first full season in the IMSA WeatherTech SportsCar Championship.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first fully electric Porsche Boxster is finally in the home stretch of development. Ahead of its official debut in early 2027, Porsche offered an early look at the two-door electric sports car.

Despite rumors that the all-electric 718 Boxster was canceled, Porsche confirmed on Tuesday that the Boxster EV will debut in the first quarter of 2027.

“Starting next year, the all-electric 718 Boxster will offer our customers a compelling entry point into the world of two-door sports cars,” Porsche CEO Dr Michael Leiters stated.

Ahead of its upcoming debut, Porsche is putting the electric sports car through the paces to ensure it preserves the DNA of its predecessors, a top priority.

Porsche developed a new “E-Core” architecture specifically for the 718 Boxster to lower the seat position and optimize weight distribution.

It has been revealed that with the 800-volt battery mounted directly behind the seats, where the internal combustion engine would typically be found, the weight is concentrated toward the middle of the vehicle. The electric Boxster has a weight distribution of 40% on the front axle and 60% on the rear, matching that of a traditional mid-engined sports car.

It also features an “intelligent lightweight construction,” as Porsche calls it, so the vehicle’s overall weight matches that of the current 911 Cabriolet models with its T-Hybrid powertrain.

“Our engineers have succeeded in transferring the Boxster’s unique concept to the electric world, further enhancing it in the process,” Porsche’s CEO said.

Recent findings suggest that the electric Boxster shares many chassis components with the 911, including the steering, which is based on the 911 Carrera GTS. It will offer rear-axle steering, a first for the 718 Boxster.

Meanwhile, the wheel and tire dimensions and braking system are based on the Porsche 911, and the electronically controlled PTV+ limited-slip differential is also pulled from the 911.

Porsche said the electric Boxster will be “the most powerful 718 ever,” but didn’t offer a specific output figure.

The range-topping Boxster EV can sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in under three seconds, according to Porsche, and it can reach a top speed of over 155 mph (250 km/h).

All electric Boxster models will be RWD and come standard with E-Shift. Like Hyundai’s performance N EVs, including the IONIQ 5 N and IONIQ 6 N, the Porsche Boxster EV features a virtual gear shift that simulates the feeling and sounds of a seven-speed PDK transmission.

When E-Shift mode is not active, the paddle can be used to toggle between three levels of recuperation.

Industry observers note that the electric Porsche 718 Boxster will make its official debut in the first quarter of 2027, so we should learn more details soon. IT will be built at Porsche’s main plant in Stuttgart-Zuffenhausen, Germany.
