📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Insideevs ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Electric Porsche Boxster Prototype Reviews Are Out. Here's What Critics Think

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Insideevs

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this is a massive moment for the auto industry.
  • Sources indicate that before we dig into what critics think, it's crucial to note the tumultuous journey the electric Boxster has had.
  • In a recent development, the overall consensus is this: It's a proper Porsche Boxster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a massive moment for the auto industry. Whether you're an EV fan, an EV doubter, or just a car enthusiast in general, the electric Porsche Boxster is a big deal. It marks the first time that a true, enthusiast-based roadster switches from piston to electric power. Its public reception will make a huge impact on the future of electric sports cars. Yesterday, that reception began. The review embargo lifted for the Boxster on Tuesday, so we can finally hear the thoughts of genuine gearheads and EV enthusiasts alike.

Sources indicate that before we dig into what critics think, it's crucial to note the tumultuous journey the electric Boxster has had. The will they/won't they discussion of whether Porsche would even build the damn thing, and whether an electric Boxster would be any good, seemed endless. There was also discussion of whether Porsche would build a gasoline Boxster alongside it, as that seemed to originally be the plan. But for now this is electric-only. So now that the electric Boxster is finally here, and Porsche has no gas-powered version to hide it behind, how is it?

In a recent development, the overall consensus is this: It's a proper Porsche Boxster. The Boxster might actually be the perfect sports car to electrify because its engine has always been secondary to its handling. A Boxster is supposed to be sharp, nimble, and thrilling on a twisty road. According to early reviews, this latest "983" generation Boxster is all of those things.

According to recent reports, "Whether you’re welcoming the Boxster’s EV transition or bemoaning the loss of its internal-combustion engines, particularly the iconic flat-six, we think anyone who drives the next-generation 983 Boxster will agree it’s fantastic. The steering, inherited from the 992.2 911 Carrera GTS, is eager and sharp, and rear-axle steering will also be available. You can feel the Boxster’s rear-biased weight distribution in the way its rear end steps out when lifting off the throttle," said Dave VanderWerp said for Car and Driver.

In a recent development, "The steering in the electric 718 Boxster is Carrera GTS good, obviously, since that’s where it’s from. Perfect weight, razor-sharp, with quick turn-in; it’s easy to place the car in and through a corner," Joel Feder wrote for The Drive. "It’s also extremely easy to kick the rear end of the electric 718 Boxster out and then control the slide through a corner. I imagine this thing will be a drift machine when given the opportunity without Porsche’s handlers watching my every move.".

Industry observers note that autocar's Illya Verpraet had similar things to say: "The classic Porsche driving position and round wheel immediately sets the mood. At the lower speeds on our sighting lap, I didn’t immediately gel with the steering, which seems a bit too eager to bring the rear-steer into play, but as soon as we picked up the pace, it came alive in the way that the best 911 steering tends to: not crazy fast or heavy, but lightning-accurate and full of feedback.".

Recent findings suggest that most reviewers also seem to note the Boxster's similarity to its gas-powered predecessor. It supposedly looks familiar inside (Porsche didn't allow photos of it, so we have to just take every reviewer's word for it), handles like a Boxster, and it feels as expensive as one.

"If you put a Boxster GTS 4.0 owner into this EV with the fake noise turned on, all they’d notice would be the slightly different interior and how much quicker the car is when they drop the hammer," stated MotorTrend's Jonny Lieberman.

And it's stated to be quick. Porsche didn't reveal exactly how much power the car has, nor which model it was. It could have been a regular Boxster, Boxster S, or even something spicier, like a Boxster GTS. Either way, this Boxster impressed with its performance, despite being a single-motor, rear-wheel drive car. That single motor pairs to a limited-slip differential, too, so it should feel pretty natural through corners for current Boxster owners.

Porsche didn't say what sort of battery powered the prototype Boxster, but we do know where the battery is. Rather than having a skateboard battery pack in the floor, Porsche stuffed it behind the driver, where the engine normally would be. That does two things. It gives the 983 the same sort of weight distribution as every other Boxster, while also allowing passengers to sit lower than a normal EV. The result is that the electric Boxster has a lower center of gravity than previous generations.

According to recent reports, overall, this new Boxster seems incredibly promising. It's fast, it's apparently very fun to drive, and it feels like a Boxster should. I can't wait to see what it's like when Porsche finally reveals it.

The next EV to plug in at a ski resort might be the one that groomed your trail. ChargePoint has struck a deal with Kässbohrer, the German company behind PistenBully snow groomers, to bring charging to ski resorts and indoor ski facilities across Europe and North America.

According to recent reports, under the agreement, Kässbohrer will connect its customers with ChargePoint for chargers, software, and support with planning, installation, and day-to-day operations. Resorts can use the same provider for the snow groomers and other vehicles they keep at the maintenance depot, as well as for the EV chargers skiers use while they’re out on the slopes.

Industry observers note that kässbohrer’s first fully electric groomer, the PistenBully 100 E, uses electric motors to move the machine and spin the tiller that smooths the snow. It has a 196 kWh battery and can handle up to three hours of normal grooming on a charge, according to the manufacturer. It can take up to 22 kW on AC or 150 kW on a DC fast charger. It fast charges from zero to 100% in about an hour.

According to recent reports, chargePoint says Kässbohrer accounts for more than half of the snow groomers sold worldwide each year. Resorts can start working with the companies now. Which resorts will install ChargePoint’s chargers first, and how many will go in, are TBC.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the November/December 2026 problem of Car and Driver.

It has been revealed that these days, I’m particularly interested in cars of the past. By that I mean the distant past. Such is the case for the 1886 Benz Patent Motorwagen I drove during Monterey Car Week. Now when someone asks, “What’s the oldest car you’ve ever driven?” I have an unassailable answer. That is, unless you’ve driven Cugnot’s steam car. You did? No way. Was it cool?

The Patent Motorwagen gets credit for being first because Carl Benz designed it to be a car from the get-go. He didn’t simply take a horse-drawn carriage, add an engine and drivetrain, subtract the horse and reins, carry the oats.

It has been revealed that I love primordial stuff because things we take for granted today had not yet been figured out. There were lots of guesses—some right, others not. Driving a vehicle that old is disorienting, challenging, and sometimes dangerous. Maybe something will explode. Maybe you’ll fall out. Boring hadn’t been engineered into the experience yet.

See all results for used cars for sale near 70802.

In a recent development, the Patent Motorwagen gives substantial perambulator vibes, and baby, I am here for it. It has only three wheels, to keep it simple and light. Carriages turned their entire axle, since uprights and kingpins at the wheels were still years away. Steering the first car involves grabbing what appears to be the wood handle of an awl—the automotive steering wheel hadn’t been invented yet either. Also not in existence in 1886: carburetor jets, engine radiators, radios, tetanus shots.

Another hitherto unimagined concept: hiding the crankshaft and flywheel behind casings. The crank, connecting rod, cam gear, and drive belt all sit out in the open. Some of those parts have to be greased up before your drive. For others, oil is metered out onto the cylinder and the intake valve by drip lubricators before it runs over less critical parts and leaves behind a greasy trail on the road.

Industry observers note that to start the Benz, switch on the ignition that sends energy to the roughly eight-inch-long spark plug, then grab the horizontal flywheel. Give that a Wheel of Fortune–worthy spin and wait. The air-hexane fuel mixture is adjustable, so you can richen it to help the car start (it originally ran on naphtha, which was available at apothecaries in 1886, right next to the laudanum). There’s no throttle, so the 1.0-liter doesn’t stray far from its 400-rpm operating speed. A 4.8-quart copper vessel perched over the engine holds the water that cools the cylinder. After about an hour of operation, the water boils over, and you stop and take a calf’s-head-stew break to let things cool.

Recent findings suggest that to accelerate, push the long lever on the left side of the leather-trimmed park bench to engage the engine-driven leather strap to the axle. Feel the 0.88 horsepower. To stop, pull that lever back to actuate a shoe that drags on the axle. Not to sound like an 1886 infomercial, but driving the Patent Motorwagen is so easy, a toddler could do it. It’ll hit a claimed 13 mph, and it was the most amazing 13 mph I’ve ever experienced. There’s no way I’m going to be this fun when I’m 140 years old.

See all results for used cars for sale near 70802.

According to recent reports, senior features editor Elana Scherr shares my fondness for the supercentenarian set. She owns a 1915 Dodge, making her the perfect person to organize a U.S. equivalent of Britain’s London-to-Brighton race for early cars. I rode along and got to exceed a 45-mph speed limit in a 116-year-old Pullman, ancient proof that speed limits are set too low. Not to worry, I was running Waze. Scherr’s account begins on page 64.

Sources indicate that if you aren’t in the mood to go antiquing, there’s a 795-hp Mustang on page 34, a nearly 1000-hp Audi super car on page 58, and the latest Corvette Grand Sport on page 72. Encompassing both new and old, this is a great issue.

Carnegie Mellon’s Buggy Is the 100-Year-Old Race Series You Never Knew About, But Won’t Be Able to Stop Watching

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, ever heard of Buggy?
  • In a recent development, to understand how this sport works from the car design to the track, Road & Track spoke with Caroline Kiesnowski, the head mechanic and driver for a team.
  • Industry observers note that “Basically, the easiest way to describe it is you put a person in a tube, and you use it as a baton in a relay race,” Kiesnowski states.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ever heard of Buggy? With a capital B? Referring to a specific type of racing? Neither had we, until recently—but where there’s racing, count Road & Track intrigued. Buggy, so you know, is a unique form of racing only taking place at Carnegie Mellon University (CMU), and it’s been happening for more than 100 years. Similar to Formula SAE, students engineer, build, and drive the vehicles that compete in the odd spectacle. And yes, in case you were questioning how the buggy is driven, someone is actually inside that tube of carbon fiber.

In a recent development, to understand how this sport works from the car design to the track, Road & Track spoke with Caroline Kiesnowski, the head mechanic and driver for a team. Currently a junior in mechanical engineering at CMU, she broke down what it takes to compete in Buggy.

Industry observers note that “Basically, the easiest way to describe it is you put a person in a tube, and you use it as a baton in a relay race,” Kiesnowski states. “You get pushed up two hills, you do a free roll where the driver is completely in control—they're steering and everything—and then you get pushed back up three more hills to a finish line.”.

It’s incredibly competitive, with lots of teams vying for the win. Just like professional motorsports, each team designs a new buggy every year using experience from years past and new digital tools to refine the vehicle. The priorities are fairly self explanatory: you want the smallest, lightest buggy possible for being pushed up the hill, then for the downhill sections, designing a buggy with the smallest coefficient of drag and wheels with minimal rolling resistance is paramount. Speeds top out around 40 miles per hour, so these little vehicles are positively cruising at their fastest pace—especially considering their pilots are a foot above the pavement.

The students who end up piloting them are highly recruited, Kiesnowski tells me. Each team wants the smallest possible buggy, which means you need a small person to design the buggy’s body around. If you watch how a driver load into their respective buggy, you’ll promptly understand how tight the squeeze is and how much the design is centered around the driver.

Recent findings suggest that while most of the course is straight or mild curves, there’s one rather challenging turn called The Chute. It’s the source of many crashes and spins, and is something students need to design their buggy around every year. Two layouts are widely used: one is the standard trike that positions two wheels in the rear and one in the front; while the other is the reverse trike, which, logically, puts two wheels up front and one in the rear.

They each have their pros and cons, but in general, the standard trike is thought to be a bit dodgier in The Chute. With only one front wheel controlling steering and turning, it’s a simple design, but ergonomics and visibility for the driver can suffer. Meanwhile, the reverse trikes most often use Ackermann-style steering, which increases complexity, but Kiesnowski finds it to be a better design for steering and braking.

Sources indicate that “The steering question is interesting because of the nature of buggy,” Kiesnowski said. “It's in a sense, proprietary information; it's historically been super-secret about people talking about their teams. Some teams even have blacked out windshields, like reflective windshields, so you can't see their steering.”.

Another challenge for the track is that said track is actually just a road, and it’s mighty bumpy. Kiesnowski recalls that teams in the past even designed suspension to give the trike a better ride, but it’s a rare design choice that adds weight to a structure you’re trying to keep as light as possible. And yes, there is passing, especially in the downhill roll section, so you could end up doing some proper wheel-to-wheel racing. As you’d expect, though, safety is the number one goal in this whole competition, so drivers have helmets, and there are regulations teams have to follow in building their vehicles to ensure the sport is as safe as possible.

As with any good motorsports event, I asked Kiesnowski about teams trying to bend the rules and regulations for an advantage. She declined to offer details, but still remarked there have indeed been instances of teams looking for an advantage beyond the book. (After all, the grand prize of pride and bragging rights over your peers is a mighty tempting trophy in college.).

In a recent development, the competition takes place every April at Carnegie Mellon’s campus in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. And while the engines are essentially members of the team pushing, it’s still a form of racing we can get excited about.

If I could only use one bike lock, it’d be this: FoldyLock Elite 110 review

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1534 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I ride e-bikes professionally, regularly testing newly introduced bikes and biking gear.
  • Of course, the name of the game in bike theft prevention is to use more than just one lock, and I’m going to return to that idea at the end of this article.
  • But for now, believe me when I say that this lock is seriously good, to the point that it has become my new primary.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I ride e-bikes professionally, regularly testing newly introduced bikes and biking gear. I don’t even own a car – I get around almost exclusively on two wheels. So when it comes to important gear like bike locks for my fleet of e-bikes, I’ve become pretty well-versed out of necessity. And after testing out the world’s strongest folding lock, the FoldyLock Elite 110, I’m more than impressed. If I could only have one lock for my e-bikes, it’d be this one.

Of course, the name of the game in bike theft prevention is to use more than just one lock, and I’m going to return to that idea at the end of this article.

But for now, believe me when I say that this lock is seriously good, to the point that it has become my new primary.

The FoldyLock Elite 110cm is identical in strength and security to the FoldyLock Forever 90cm that I tested a few years ago, yet is 20 cm (8 inches) longer, reaching 110 cm (43 inches).

Industry observers note that the FoldyLock Forever 90 and FoldyLock Elite 110 are the strongest folding locks in the world, confirmed by the premier international lock certification organization ART. These are the only folding locks that have ever achieved a 3-star ART certification. The scale goes up to 5, but 4-star and 5-star certifications are motorcycle-level locks.

To make things even more impressive, the FoldyLock line achieved that ART 3-star rating three years ago, and no other lock manufacturer has matched it on a folding lock since.

If one independent and international lock testing association isn’t enough for you, the lock is also Sold Secure GOLD rated, which is just one step below Sold Secure’s highest ever rating for bike locks.

Again, more on that at the end of this article to get you to that last step for top security.

It has been revealed that there are a lot of different styles of locks out there, and each has its own advantages and disadvantages. But as someone who rides e-bikes every day as his job, I’ve come to the opinion that a strong folding lock has the best combination of maximizing advantages and minimizing disadvantages.

For starters, folding locks allow you to lock to larger diameter anchors that would be impossible for U-locks (trees, telephone poles, multiple fence bars, etc). They’re more compact than chain locks of comparable security, both in size and weight. They’re significantly stronger than cable locks (when made with quality materials). And they mount more easily to a bike frame than nearly any other lock style, as they fold tightly and usually come with a holster.

Industry observers note that yes, there are disadvantages too. The segments mean they can’t form as close to a circle as a chain, meaning the maximum size of the tree or telephone pole you’re locking to is slightly smaller than for an equal length chain. And they usually aren’t quite as strong as U-Locks made with angle-grinder-resistant materials. But for their size and convenience, they make perhaps the best single style of lock for the best pairing of strength and convenience.

Industry observers note that since I began testing the FoldyLock Elite 110, I’ve been living with it as my main e-bike lock. I test a lot of locks, and most go onto the shelf when I’m done as backups or to give to friends/family. But the FoldyLock Elite 110 has stayed as my fresh primary lock, and here’s why.

First of all, as I mentioned, it’s the strongest folding lock in the world, as confirmed by multiple independent testing organizations. So if you want the advantages of a folding lock, there’s simply none more secure than this.

But beyond that, the FoldyLock Elite 110 is covered by multiple patents, including the specialized protected rivets that prevent nut splitter attacks and that take out any squeaks or rattles that are common in other folding locks. The lock also physically locks into its holster, which keeps it both secure (no bounce-outs) and helps keep it silent during the ride. There’s even a coating on the hardened steel segments to protect my bike frame from scratches and resist corrosion during winter use (plus a shutter on the locking mechanism for additional winter corrosion resistance).

Basically, it seems like the company has taken pretty much all of the learnings from previous locks in their lineup, and applied those lessons to the FoldyLock Elite, making it a perfect combination of strength, security, and convenience.

As I mentioned, after my time testing the FoldyLock Elite, I can say for sure that if I could only use one bike lock, it would be this one.

Industry observers note that but I don’t just use one bike lock. And I recommend you don’t either, if you can swing it.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve long known that the best way to keep your bike safe from thieves is to use two bike locks. It’s partly for the extra security, and partly for the extra time it takes a thief to work on defeating two locks, meaning they’re more likely to choose a different sucker’s bike to steal.

Recent findings suggest that I always recommend using two different styles of bike locks. Think: folding lock plus U-lock, or U-lock plus chain lock, or chain lock plus cable lock, or cable lock plus folding lock, etc. You get the idea.

According to recent reports, my FoldyLock Elite is now my primary lock, and it allows me to lock onto just about everything on the street, from official bike racks to chunky utility poles. For my secondary, I use a SeatyLock Mason 220. This U-lock is actually one step higher-rated by Sold Secure, reaching that testing organization’s Diamond level – its highest level of security rating.

Sources indicate that when I can lock both the folding lock and U-lock to an anchor, I do it. But sometimes, when I’m forced to lock to something wide like a lamppost, I lock the frame and rear wheel with the FoldyLock Elite 110, then lock the front wheel to the frame with the Mason 220 U-lock, as seen in the photo above.

In a recent development, that keeps both of my wheels and my bike locked. Despite there only being one lock keeping the bike in place to the anchor (lamppost), the second lock adds an extra layer of frustration for a thief and is likely to convince them to just choose the next bike on the sidewalk.

Industry observers note that that’s why I always recommend using two different locks, and ideally of different styles. I believe the FoldyLock Elite 110 offers the most advantages, but its few disadvantages are offset by a secondary lock, such as a strong U-lock.

When it comes to mounting, I’ve got the holster mounted onto my fork using the supplied flexible mounting straps.

Normally you’d mount it to one of your bottle mounts, but I only have a single set of bottle bosses on my e-bike’s frame, and they are at the moment taken up by a water bottle holder (surprise!).

I found that despite adding 1.9 kg or 4.1 lb to the side of my fork, my bike still rides just fine. The advantage of a rigid frame is that there’s not really much change to the unsprung mass since everything is unsprung!

I love riding hands-free in the city, and it did take me a day or two to get used to the slightly altered steering moment, but I can still ride my bike hands-free even with the extra weight there on the side of the fork.

At some point I might shift the holster onto the rear rack or swap it out for my bottle holder in favor of a fresh bottle spot, but so far it’s working great there and hasn’t caused me any handling issues.

Sources indicate that when it comes to value, I think the FoldyLock Elite 110 takes the cake here, too. It’s normally priced at an MSRP of $145, though it’s right now on sale for $119 as part of the Black Friday promotions.

It has been revealed that as I stated, I test hundreds of bikes and dozens of locks as my day job. I live and breathe bikes. The fact that this lock has become my go-to everyday lock is pretty much all you need to know about how impressive it truly is. It’s a pleasure to live with and use, which means that I actually end up using it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Volkswagen is moving back to more physical buttons, after suffering some backlash from its touch-button-heavy design. Mercedes also publicly recognized that maybe the world went too far with touchscreens. Audi, too, seems to be eyeing more physical controls. But it isn't giving up its touchscreen ones to do so. The tech giant just patented a technology that lets it have its cake and eat it, too, but creating a physical button panel that can hide behind a touchscreen.

Recent findings suggest that unearthed by CarMoses, this patent shows off a little button bar, which is just a strip of physical buttons and possibly one knob that lives below the touchscreen. At the press of a button, or even with voice control, the button bar can hide away behind the touchscreen, for anyone who prefers a simpler looking cabin. Once the buttons are hidden, the touchscreen creates a duplicate set of icons at the bottom, so button functionality isn't lost while hidden.

According to recent reports, what sort of physical buttons will occupy such a button bar? There seems to be a circular knob in the center of the buttons, so that will likely be volume. The flanking buttons could be for climate control, maybe heated seats, or perhaps even some drive mode buttons. Whatever they end up being, it will be nice to see Audi's with high-quality physical buttons again.

In the '90s, 2000s, and 2010s, Audi had some of the best buttons, switches, and knobs in the industry, all with satisfying, high-quality clicks. The current crop of piano-black plastic touch buttons in most modern Audis feels like a slap in the face for fans of the brand. So to see the return of some buttons in places where they can be easily memorized and adjusted without looking would be wonderful.

In a recent development, obviously, Audi can't use physical buttons for everything. There are far too many controls and features in modern cars for that to work. There'd be hundreds of buttons on the dashboard if that were the case. But the main buttons, the ones you use everyday, should be physical. And the beauty of this patent is that it, if you like a more high-tech vibe, you can hide them away. With this patent, Audi gets to make both camps happy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the first Switch 2 jailbreaks arrived just over a month ago, and we've already reached Nintendo's nightmare scenario: dumped games can now be played on hacked consoles. That means the door to piracy on the console is already swinging wide open, and if history is any indication it's going to be very difficult for Nintendo or its lawyers to get it closed again.

Industry observers note that A hacker called Olmectron has released a tool called nx2-relink, which can be used to turn a Switch 2 game dump into a homebrew program that can run on a jailbroken console. As noted by hacking and homebrew site GTAtemp, this is an early and experimental piece of software, so compatibility is limited right now and you will run a risk of bricking your console by using it.

Industry observers note that strictly speaking, there's nothing illegal in using the tool as advertised, making backups of games you own and have dumped yourself, though any jailbroken console risks a ban from online services by Nintendo. Olmectron says the tool includes "no games, no keys and no Nintendo files, and it won't get them for you." But, as far as I can tell, there's nothing preventing you from using this newfound power to simply download other people's dumps and use them on your console – which is the very definition of piracy.

nx2-relink features heavy contributions from Claude, as with many recent breakthroughs in the console hacking and homebrew scene. AI is dramatically increasing the pace at which developers can break through console security measures, and this isn't even the only Switch 2 backup tool to appear in the past 24 hours. A separate dev demonstrated a console booting a dumped version of Donkey Kong Bananza just yesterday, "opening the flood gates" to a upcoming era of Switch 2 hacks.

And, well, yes – the flood gates do seem to be wide open, and this trickle of dumping tools is likely a warning for the absolute tsunami of Switch 2 piracy that's likely to follow.

  • See all results for new 2026 Lexus ES for sale near 85251.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that welcome to Car and Driver’s Testing Hub, where we zoom in on the test numbers. We’ve been pushing vehicles to their limits since 1956 to provide objective data to bolster our subjective impressions (you can see how we test here).

The debut of the 2026 Lexus ES brought a full overhaul to the luxury sedan, which included a revamped hybrid variant. The fresh generation comes with fresh styling, a longer wheelbase, and an updated powertrain. In our testing, a 2026 ES350h was considerably quicker than a 2023 Lexus ES300h F Sport Handling, which was the last ES hybrid we tested.

See all results for new 2026 Lexus ES for sale near 85251.

It has been revealed that in our recent test of the ES350h, the updated sedan sprinted to 60 mph in 6.6 seconds, while the 2023 car more or less jogged its way to the 60-mph mark in 7.9 seconds. That’s a huge improvement, and one that took us by surprise, given that the new car doesn’t look drastically more powerful than the old one on paper. That’s to say nothing of the additional 352 pounds of weight in the new car either.

So, where did all the extra quickness come from? Well, we can think of several places. For starters, the 2026 ES hybrid is more powerful, even if the numbers don’t jump off the page. The powertrain, which features a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine, now churns out 244 horsepower, up from 215 in the 2023 ES. Along with a more powerful engine, the updated hybrid system uses a larger and more powerful electric drive motor than the previous generation. Lexus also now offers the gas-electric ES with all-wheel drive for the first time, and that’s the version we tested, with the additional traction helping offset the new car’s weight gain.

The new generation also moved from a 3.39:1 axle ratio to a 3.44:1 axle ratio, a change that increases low-end torque at the wheels and makes the newer car somewhat punchier off the line. Lastly, the 2026 car gets a larger hybrid battery that can provide more horsepower than the smaller unit in the previous ES.

None of the changes are individually earth-shattering—especially with the extra 352 pounds of weight—but add them together, and the ES hybrid is a much quicker car than before.

  • The first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the upcoming maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content. Now, the developer has revealed how it plans to use some of that time, and the first port of call is Battlefield Labs.

As discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a massive component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

The first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the upcoming maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2. BF Studios says the map falls between Eastwood and Mirak Valley, in terms of size.

Recent findings suggest that the blog post even likened it to Battlefield 1’s St. Quentin Scar, and Battlefield 5’s Arras. Although we’ve yet to actually play it, the size and description do sound really well, especially in a game as starved of massive maps as Battlefield 6 currently is.

Another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

More Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off newly introduced gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

Industry observers note that battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios mentioned we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Recent findings suggest that ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

There’s even more exciting news for fans of big maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is right now in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

It has been revealed that for context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its complications elsewhere, and BF Studios claims it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

Finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

Redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.

#132466. Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1237 w)

Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1237 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A ketogenic diet may offer significant health benefits beyond weight loss, according to a new clinical trial that compared three popular approaches to eating.
  • The results were especially striking for people with prediabetes.
  • In a recent development, "We know weight loss can improve metabolic health in people who are obese," indicates Samuel Klein, the study's corresponding author at Washington University School of Medicine in St.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A ketogenic diet may offer significant health benefits beyond weight loss, according to a new clinical trial that compared three popular approaches to eating. Researchers found that people following a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet experienced substantially greater reductions in liver fat than those eating Mediterranean or low-fat diets, even though all three groups lost similar amounts of weight.

The results were especially striking for people with prediabetes. After just four to five months on a ketogenic (or "Keto") diet, approximately half of the participants no longer met the diagnostic criteria for the condition. The findings, published in the journal Cell Metabolism, suggest that the types of foods people eat can influence metabolic health in ways that extend beyond the number of pounds they lose.

In a recent development, "We know weight loss can improve metabolic health in people who are obese," indicates Samuel Klein, the study's corresponding author at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, Missouri. "Our data suggest that if you have high liver fat content and prediabetes, reducing carbohydrate intake can have important therapeutic effects on metabolism beyond just weight loss alone.".

Comparing Keto, Mediterranean, and Low-Fat Diets.

An estimated 40% of American adults have obesity, a condition associated with increased risks of type 2 diabetes, fatty liver disease, and other health problems. Doctors frequently recommend dietary changes to help patients lose weight and improve their metabolic health, which refers to how effectively the body manages energy, blood sugar, and fats.

Industry observers note that three commonly recommended approaches are low-carbohydrate diets, low-fat diets, and Mediterranean diets. Although each can support weight loss, researchers have been uncertain whether one offers additional metabolic advantages when the amount of weight lost is roughly the same.

These eating patterns differ substantially in their nutritional makeup. Low-carbohydrate approaches, including Atkins and ketogenic diets, restrict carbohydrate consumption, while low-fat diets may obtain as much as 70% of their calories from carbohydrates. The Mediterranean diet emphasizes plant foods such as vegetables, nuts, and olive oil, along with moderate amounts of fish and dairy. Ketogenic diets, meanwhile, can include considerable amounts of fat from animal products, including saturated fat.

According to recent reports, to compare their effects, Klein and his colleagues recruited 42 adults with obesity, prediabetes, and fatty liver disease. Prediabetes occurs when blood sugar levels rise above the normal range but have not yet reached the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Fatty liver disease involves excess fat accumulating inside liver cells, which can interfere with the body's ability to regulate metabolism.

A Controlled Clinical Trial With Similar Weight Loss.

Participants were randomly assigned to follow one of three diets: ketogenic, Mediterranean, or a low-fat diet emphasizing plant-based foods. To ensure that participants followed their assigned eating looks, the research team supplied all their meals and arranged weekly consultations with a dietitian.

The diets had sharply different proportions of carbohydrates and fat. In the ketogenic group, carbohydrates accounted for just 4% of daily calories, while fat supplied 73%. The Mediterranean group received 50% of its calories from carbohydrates and 35% from fat. The plant-forward group consumed 70% of its calories from carbohydrates and 15% from fat.

It has been revealed that researchers adjusted calorie intake individually so that participants across all three groups lost approximately 10% of their starting body weight. Reaching this target took about four to five months.

By the end of the intervention, every group had experienced meaningful reductions in body fat and improvements in insulin sensitivity. Insulin is the hormone that helps move sugar from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy. Greater insulin sensitivity makes it easier for the body to maintain healthy blood sugar levels.

However, the similarities between the groups largely ended there.

Keto Diet Reduces Liver Fat by 67%.

The ketogenic diet produced the largest improvements in several vital indicators of liver function and metabolic health.

It has been revealed that participants following keto experienced an average 67% reduction in liver fat, compared with a 45% reduction in both the Mediterranean and low-fat groups. Because the groups lost comparable amounts of weight, the difference suggests that carbohydrate restriction may influence liver fat through mechanisms beyond weight loss alone.

To investigate these effects, the researchers collected blood samples repeatedly over a 24-hour period, allowing them to observe changes in hormones involved in energy metabolism.

The ketogenic group showed the greatest increase in glucagon, a hormone that helps regulate the body's energy supply and promotes the reduction of fat stored in the liver. Participants on keto also experienced the largest decrease in insulin levels, another change that can help reduce liver fat accumulation.

One result was particularly unexpected. Despite getting nearly three-quarters of their calories from fat, the keto participants did not show an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels during the study.

"The most surprising finding was that participants in the ketogenic diet group didn't experience an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels despite consuming the most fat," indicates Max Petersen, the study's first author at Washington University School of Medicine.

Half of Keto Participants No Longer Had Prediabetes.

In a recent development, the benefits extended beyond liver fat. After the weight-loss intervention, approximately 50% of participants assigned to the ketogenic diet no longer met the criteria for prediabetes. By comparison, that milestone was reached by 29% of those on the Mediterranean diet and just 7% of those following the low-fat, plant-forward diet.

It has been revealed that these differences are notable because prediabetes signals an elevated risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Bringing blood sugar levels below the prediabetes threshold is an important improvement, although it does not necessarily mean the condition has been permanently reversed.

It has been revealed that the findings also highlight a potentially notable distinction in weight management: losing weight and improving metabolic health are closely connected, but they are not necessarily the same thing. The composition of a diet may affect how the body handles blood sugar, stores fat, and responds to hormones, even when weight loss is similar.

Sources indicate that researchers emphasize the growing importance of understanding these effects as powerful new obesity treatments become more widely available. GLP-1 medications, which act on hormone pathways involved in appetite and blood sugar regulation, have transformed the treatment of obesity by helping many patients achieve substantial weight loss.

"GLP-1-based medications have revolutionized the therapy of obesity. We now have a very effective pharmacotherapy for achieving significant weight loss," Petersen says. "But in addition, our study shows that the specific composition of the diet can give you added benefits.".

Sources indicate that although the trial was relatively small and lasted only four to five months, its carefully controlled design offers evidence that dietary composition can play an crucial role in metabolic health. Longer studies involving more participants will be needed to determine whether the benefits persist and how different diets compare over time.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health and the Foundation for Barnes-Jewish Hospital.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • While it may be the luxury offshoot of Honda, Acura’s cars have never actually been sold in Japan in any official capacity.
  • Sources indicate that that finally changes today.
  • According to recent reports, acura has been teasing the possibility of the Integra Type S reaching the Japanese market all year, starting with a production model conspicuously on display among Honda’s Tokyo Auto Salon offerings in January.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While it may be the luxury offshoot of Honda, Acura’s cars have never actually been sold in Japan in any official capacity. The luxury automaker has been focused on North America for almost the entirety of its four decades of existence, meaning that any Acura cars in the brand’s would-be home country are either imported or modified cars initially sold as Hondas.

Sources indicate that that finally changes today. As of Wednesday, the Acura Integra Type S is now on sale in Japan, fulfilling a promise made earlier this year. In addition to being the first Acura to reach that market, it is the first variant of the new Integra to be sold outside of North America in any form.

According to recent reports, acura has been teasing the possibility of the Integra Type S reaching the Japanese market all year, starting with a production model conspicuously on display among Honda’s Tokyo Auto Salon offerings in January. The Integra was shown again at another Japanese show in February before production aims were confirmed in March. Now, Japanese buyers will actually be able to get their hands on the Ohio-built Integra.

The Acura shares an engine and many other parts with the Honda Civic Type R, but the pair diverge in a few key ways. While the Integra is softer and more refined, the Honda is sharper and more harsh. American buyers could pick freely between the two, but other markets have not had the option to do so until now. It’s good news for Japanese enthusiasts looking for a slightly different flavor of performance Honda—a list that includes noted Integra Type S fan Yuki Tsunoda.

Fred Smith's love of cars comes from his fascination with auto racing. Unfortunately, that passion led him to daily drive a high-mileage, first-year Porsche Panamera. He is still thinking about the last lap of the 2011 Indianapolis 500.

Europe Gets This Tiny Latest Suzuki EV. It Makes A Mini Look Substantial

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Insideevs

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • car market in 2012, but it still builds the kind of small hatchbacks European buyers have long favored, now also powered by electricity.
  • The Ignis is Suzuki’s first subcompact electric car developed for global markets, but its roots are in Japan.
  • A 26-kilowatt-hour lithium iron phosphate battery sits under the floor of Suzuki’s dedicated Heartect-e electric platform.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Suzuki left the U.S. car market in 2012, but it still builds the kind of small hatchbacks European buyers have long favored, now also powered by electricity. Its latest is the Ignis EV, a city car that measures just 11 feet 9 inches long (3.57 meters). It’s due in Europe in summer 2027, when it will face a fresh generation of small EVs from both European and Chinese automakers.

The Ignis is Suzuki’s first subcompact electric car developed for global markets, but its roots are in Japan. The company recently debuted the e Sky there, an electric kei car that supplies the basis for the Ignis’s body and powertrain. The Ignis still has the typical kei proportions (it's tall and narrow), but Suzuki says it took the car onto European city streets and winding roads to tune the suspension and power delivery, making it more appealing to the people it hopes will buy one.

A 26-kilowatt-hour lithium iron phosphate battery sits under the floor of Suzuki’s dedicated Heartect-e electric platform. Yes, that really is what it's called. Up front, the motor, inverter, and reduction gears share a single compact assembly that sends 90 horsepower and 98 pound-feet (133 Nm) to the front wheels. Suzuki indicates it chose LFP for safety and longevity, but it hasn’t given the European car a range or charging figure yet.

Recent findings suggest that the Ignis EV has a very tight 29.5-foot (9-meter) turning circle. Its overhangs are tiny, giving it a wheel-at-each-corner stance that looks unique while maximizing available interior room. The LED signatures at both ends take their shape from digital numerals, and the dark pillars give the roof a floating look.

It has been revealed that inside, a curve runs from the dashboard into the doors, with a wide display and a ceramic-inspired storage tray across the dash. Suzuki President Toshihiro Suzuki credits the firm’s decades of building Japanese mini vehicles for its ability to provide a genuinely usable cabin in such a small footprint.

For decades, European brands had most of this business to themselves. If you wanted an inexpensive car that could squeeze down a narrow street, Fiat would happily sell you a Panda, Renault a Twingo and Volkswagen an Up. Chinese automakers see an opening as those buyers go electric.

Sources indicate that leapmotor brought the T03 to Europe through its partnership with Stellantis, while BYD adapted its Chinese-market Seagull for Europe and called it the Dolphin Surf. Driving the latter, what stood out to me was how well it drove, how little felt cheap, and how much kit it had for its sub-€20,000 starting price.

It has been revealed that by the time the Ignis arrives next year, European buyers will have had plenty of practice shopping for small EVs. Renault has revived both the 5 and the Twingo as electric cars, and there’s also the related Dacia Spring. Volkswagen has the ID. Polo, Cupra has the Raval, and Skoda has the Epiq, and there definitely seems to be demand for them. In September, a major VW dealer group reported more than 30,000 orders for the ID. Polo and a waiting list stretching to ten months.

That leaves one substantial question for the little Suzuki. What will it cost? Consider the redesigned Dacia Spring. Dacia moved production from China to Slovenia, shared the electric Twingo’s underpinnings, and produced a car that starts at €17,900 in Italy. It gets up to 155 miles (250 kilometers) of WLTP range from a battery only slightly larger than the one in the Ignis.

📅 26 Jan 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (374 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Vg247

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, after weeks of waiting, Arc Raiders developer Embark has officially unveiled the first few months of the game’s 2026 roadmap.
  • It has been revealed that we’re expecting a content update each month, with the majority of the biggest additions happening on the game’s existing maps.
  • It has been revealed that while we wait for that, Arc Raiders is going to go through several events and other in-game changes, some more meaningful (and exciting) than others.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, after weeks of waiting, Arc Raiders developer Embark has officially unveiled the first few months of the game’s 2026 roadmap. The initiative is split into four months, covering January to April, collectively dubbed Escalation.

It has been revealed that we’re expecting a content update each month, with the majority of the biggest additions happening on the game’s existing maps. There is, however, at least one new map in the works, but it won’t be here until sometime in April.

It has been revealed that while we wait for that, Arc Raiders is going to go through several events and other in-game changes, some more meaningful (and exciting) than others. January looks to be the lightest so far, which makes sense given that it’s just a week or so from ending.

January’s chapter is titled Headwinds, kicking off on January 27. This segment will see the addition of a fresh matchmaking option for players above level 40 - at or near the game’s endgame. We’re also expecting a new Map Condition, and a new Player Project for everyone to contribute to.

Things start getting interesting in February, when Shrouded Sky will begin. This chapter brings three exciting additions to Arc Raiders. There will be a fresh Map Condition, new Arc Threat, and the start of another Player Project.

Interestingly, we’re going to see some sort of map update during the month, but Embark didn’t share anymore details. The next Raider Deck will also deploy in February, alongside a new Expedition Window.

The Flashpoint chapter begins in March, when we’re expecting another new Map Condition, one more new Arc Threat, as well as another Player Project. March’s most interesting addition is an update to everyone’s trusty rooster friend, Scrappy.

Finally, April is when the big guns come out, because that’s when the first new map of 2026 will arrive in Arc Raiders. With it, comes a new large Arc, which is to be expected. A new Map Condition will debut then, too, likely starting off on the new map.

That’s pretty much it, but seeing as we’re just one day away from the start of the January stage, things are about to get exciting again in Arc Raiders.

#132459. Breaking: Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1315 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Plastic is used in everything from food packaging and water bottles to children's toys, largely because it is considered chemically stable and unlikely to react with its surroundings.
  • In a recent development, as larger plastic objects fragment into microplastics and even smaller nanoplastics, the amount of exposed surface area increases dramatically.
  • Researchers at Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley identified the chemical processes behind this phenomenon in a latest study published in Nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Plastic is used in everything from food packaging and water bottles to children's toys, largely because it is considered chemically stable and unlikely to react with its surroundings. However, new research suggests that this assumption may not hold when plastic breaks down into extremely small particles.

In a recent development, as larger plastic objects fragment into microplastics and even smaller nanoplastics, the amount of exposed surface area increases dramatically. Scientists have now discovered that these newly exposed surfaces can interact with water in unexpected ways, producing reactive molecules that may harm living cells.

Researchers at Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley identified the chemical processes behind this phenomenon in a latest study published in Nature. Their findings challenge the longstanding idea that microplastics are simply passive fragments of material.

"As plastic fragments into smaller and smaller particles, its surface area increases enormously. Then microplastics change the water that surrounds them, generating high-energy, reactive radicals (reactive oxygen species, ROS) that very likely contribute to biological damage that we see in animals and potentially in humans as a result of microplastic exposure," mentioned Wei Min, a Columbia professor of Chemistry and Biomedical Engineering.

Why Microplastics Could Be Dangerous Inside the Human Body.

The discovery raises important questions about what happens when microplastics enter the human body. Blood and cells contain large amounts of water, creating conditions in which these tiny particles could continue participating in chemical reactions.

In a recent development, rather than remaining inactive after exposure, microplastics may generate reactive oxygen species, often called ROS. These highly reactive molecules can damage biological structures, including components of cells and tissues. The findings offer a possible explanation for some of the harmful effects associated with microplastic exposure, although they do not establish that this process causes specific diseases in humans.

The research builds on earlier work by Min's laboratory that helped reveal just how widespread microscopic plastic contamination has become.

According to recent reports, in a widely reported 2024 study, the Columbia researchers developed a laser-based microscopy technique capable of detecting extremely small plastic particles. Using this technology, they found an average of approximately 240,000 detectable plastic fragments in a single liter of bottled water (mostly nanometer-sized plastic, nanoplastics). That was 10 to 100 times more particles than previous estimates had suggested.

The discovery helped draw greater attention to the presence of microplastics and nanoplastics throughout the food system.

Growing Concerns About Microplastics and Human Health.

Since that earlier research attracted widespread attention, the potential health consequences of microplastic exposure have become an increasingly important public health issue.

In 2026, the federal government launched a $144 million initiative focused on addressing toxic microplastics in the human body. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also added microplastics to a federal list of contaminants that may be of concern in drinking water, marking their first appearance on the list.

Meanwhile, studies published in major scientific journals, including the Fresh England Journal of Medicine, Nature Medicine, and Nature Health, have reported associations between exposure to microplastics and nanoplastics and serious conditions such as heart attacks, strokes, dementia, and brain tumors.

However, an crucial question has remained unanswered. If plastic is generally considered chemically inert, how might these microscopic fragments contribute to biological damage?

The latest findings identify a previously overlooked chemical pathway that could help researchers understand these potential health risks.

Sources indicate that "Our research found that when microplastics interact with water, as they do when they're in bottled water, or when they're absorbed into our bloodstream, they spontaneously generate what we call reactive oxygen species (ROS)," said Naixin Qian, a postdoctoral researcher in Wei Min's lab who helped lead the research. "ROS are textbook examples of the kinds of molecules that can damage animal and human tissue.".

How Water Triggers Harmful Chemical Reactions.

One of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is that water plays an active role in the reaction.

Sources indicate that many plastics are hydrophobic, meaning their surfaces repel water. When water encounters these surfaces, the molecules and electrically charged particles near the boundary can behave differently than they do in ordinary water.

The researchers found that these interactions can encourage electrons to move between chemical species, allowing highly reactive radicals to form. As plastic fragments become smaller, their greater surface area provides more locations where these reactions can occur.

Sources indicate that "Water is a key active player here, rather than just a spectator. It's integral to making these microplastics reactive. Water molecules become chemically active when they come into contact with plastic, which is hydrophobic. Contact between the water and plastic creates an environment that facilitates electron transfer, and the formation of reactive radicals. When plastics fragment into smaller particles, their increasing surface-to-volume ratio creates more of these chemically active areas," Min remarked.

In a recent development, to investigate the process, the Columbia researchers performed chemical and biological experiments. Their collaborators in Professor Teresa Head-Gordon's laboratory at UC Berkeley used theoretical calculations and computer simulations to examine the interactions between plastic surfaces and water at the molecular level.

It has been revealed that the Berkeley team developed a theoretical explanation showing how hydroxide ions, which are negatively charged particles, can become concentrated in the layers of water immediately surrounding a water-repelling plastic surface. In this environment, the ions can more readily lose electrons and form hydroxyl radicals.

In a recent development, hydroxyl radicals are particularly reactive chemical species capable of damaging biological molecules. Their formation provides a possible link between the physical breakdown of plastics and the biological effects researchers have observed.

Could the Discovery Lead to Safer Plastics?

Understanding the chemistry involved could eventually help scientists develop plastics that are less likely to generate harmful reactive molecules when exposed to water.

"Our fundamental work that the most hydrophobic microplastics interacting with water can drive chemical reactivity could ultimately lead to new engineering solutions by redesigning the chemistry of these commodity plastics to reduce the toxic outcomes on health and the environment," stated Head-Gordon.

It has been revealed that the implications also extend beyond human health. Microplastics can enter rivers, lakes, and other waterways through industrial waste, wastewater, and everyday activities. The newly identified chemical reactions could influence aquatic organisms and ecosystems exposed to these particles.

It has been revealed that co-author Beizhan Yan of Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory emphasized that microplastics can originate from numerous sources, including plastic manufacturing facilities and laundromats. Everyday processes, such as heating materials in a microwave or leaving bottled water exposed to sunlight during storage, can also contribute to the formation of tiny plastic particles.

"This work has significant implications for environmental and human health," said co-author Beizhan Yan of Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "In certain environments, such as discharges from plastic manufacturers and laundromats, microplastics can form and enter aquatic environments. This work also indicates that radicals can form on hydrophobic plastic surfaces in water, which could affect ecosystems and human health following exposure. In addition, various uses and processes in our daily lives can generate microplastics, including microwave heating, sunlight exposure of bottled water during storage. This foundational work provides a potential pathway for understanding their health impacts.".

Recent findings suggest that by revealing that microplastics can actively alter the chemistry of surrounding water, the research adds a new dimension to concerns about plastic pollution. It also establishes a potential mechanism for investigating how these widespread particles interact with living systems, while opening the door to strategies for reducing their environmental and health risks.

Materials provided by Columbia University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#132458. A Change of Tune: How the 2000s Changed How We Listen to Music in Cars

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (711 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Roadandtrack ↗ Open Full Page

A Change of Tune: How the 2000s Changed How We Listen to Music in Cars

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These days, each of us is in our own little world.
  • This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.
  • In a recent development, once we shook off Y2K anxiety, the new millennium began as normal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These days, each of us is in our own little world. We’ve forfeited a largely shared reality and replaced it with an almost infinite series of more private universes. And I’m going to be honest with you: Results have been mixed. The seeds of our collective solitude were planted in the decades before, and the worst of it wouldn’t hit us until the years after, but 2000–09 was the era when the monoculture really began to fracture and fragment into microcultures. The great American mainstream was dwindling in the Aughts, a narrative expressed through our music. Newly introduced technology changed the way people across the world listened. And as Americans, we in particular experienced this historic shift through our car stereos.

This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.

In a recent development, once we shook off Y2K anxiety, the new millennium began as normal. Fueled by boy bands, blockbuster hip-hop, and, somehow, Limp Bizkit, the recording industry was flush in 2000. What was big was huge, and whether you liked the songs or not, you knew them. My main musical memory of the year 2000 took place in a rental car, on a drive up to the mountains with my roommates. The mid-size sedan had a mere cassette player, so we made do with the radio. On that October afternoon, some station played the comeback single from a band that hadn’t released a studio album in three years: U2’s “Beautiful Day.” We turned it up, we nodded along, and we were impressed that a band could sound this good despite having members who were now 40. Best of all, we shared the experience with however many strangers were also tuned in to this frequency.

As the Aughts progressed, I found myself sliding into my car’s CD slot fewer store-bought discs and more homemade mixes I burned using my iBook after downloading music from iTunes. It was easy, it was cheap at 99 cents per song, and it was as frictionless as a click on the touchpad. I recently found a box of these discs in my garage, and each one is packed with music I have not thought about since I put them there. These early-­Aughts songs left me no physical album covers to remember them by; the playlists were not yet saved for posterity on streaming services. They vanished.

Then there was the iPod. Other MP3 players predated it, but the iPod was sleek and sexy and held up to 1000 songs, which I swear sounded like a lot in 2001. The forward-thinking among us might carry a special cord in our bag in case we found ourselves in a car with an auxiliary input. Traditional radio stations suffered as we ditched the DJs and did their job for free.

Satellite radio rolled out an effort to fill the void—XM in 2001, Sirius in 2002, then SiriusXM in 2008, with hundreds of hyperspecific-genre stations on the digital dial. Satellite radio broke us in to the concept of paying a monthly fee to listen to music we don’t own, and Spotify and Apple Music would run with that idea in the decades ahead. Now we all have access to virtually every piece of music ever recorded, but who is guiding us through it? It’s chaos. I find myself longing for those days before endless choices, before Bluetooth or aux cables, when I’d trust a stranger to play something for me while I was driving. When I’d be on a road trip and an unknown station would fuzz in and play a country song and a public service announcement, when a human being in a studio remarked something that streaked on radio waves across the desert air, and we were connected, until the station fuzzed out.

In a recent development, of course, I can still do that. But the convenience culture that has continued to creep in since the Aughts has conditioned me to pull out my phone, wirelessly connect it to the car, and put on a mix or a podcast. I actually have to remind myself that those days were real, when the radio was once our go-to.

I miss those times. The newly introduced stuff from U2 is pretty good, though.

  • Industry observers note that the firm, which usually charges an average of $0.40/kilowatt-hour, is now asking for $0.20/kWh plus tax at all its DC fast charging stations in the United States.
  • For long-distance travel, the slashed charging rates can make a big difference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ionna, the EV charging network that ranked first in J.D. Power’s latest public charging satisfaction survey, has slashed prices at its stations across the country for Thanksgiving weekend.

Industry observers note that the firm, which usually charges an average of $0.40/kilowatt-hour, is now asking for $0.20/kWh plus tax at all its DC fast charging stations in the United States. That’s a 50% discount, and drivers don’t have to do anything special to get it—just plug in and pay, either through the automaker’s official smartphone app, the on-site payment terminals, or the Presto app for Tesla owners who want to enjoy the Autocharge function.

For long-distance travel, the slashed charging rates can make a big difference. A single 50-kilowatt-hour session that used to cost $20 will now be just $10 plus tax, but seeing how many people are traveling across the country these days, multiple sessions will be necessary, driving the cost savings even further.

Sources indicate that and it’s not like the cost reduction comes with any strings attached. Ionna uses 400-kilowatt chargers from Alpitronic exclusively, so there’s plenty of wiggle room for even the most power-hungry EVs out there. What’s more, many stalls have dual cords for each port, with a CCS2 connector and a NACS connector, so charging adapters aren’t needed at most locations.

Separately, Ionna has discounts for several automakers, including Mercedes-Benz, BMW, General Motors, and Stellantis.

The charging operator installed its first stalls in 2024, and it has wasted no time expanding its footprint promptly. On its second anniversary, Ionna celebrated by opening its 100th site, and the company now has 229 sites and nearly 1,900 ports nationwide, according to the Department of Energy's Alternative Fuels Data Center (AFDC). Still, the charging network is not slowing down, with dozens of locations under construction and looks to introduce 500-kW chargers in the near future.

Most EV brands support Plug & Charge at Ionna, with Tesla recently getting Autocharge functionality through a third-party smartphone application. Ionna itself doesn’t have a smartphone app, instead relying on automakers and third-party apps to integrate its locations. So far, this approach has turned out to be quite successful, with J.D. Power’s latest public charging survey putting the operator first, ahead of Tesla and the rest of the competition.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that marvel Cosmic Invasion was a bit of a dream game for me; I loved the X-Men arcade game in the '90s, so when Tribute Games released the excellent Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder's Revenge in 2022, I immediately hoped they'd revitalize other licensed brawler franchises released by Konami in the late '80s and early '90s. While we still haven't heard any word of a latest brawler starring The Simpsons, Tribute did follow up its Turtle triumph with Marvel Cosmic Invasion, another throwback side-scrolling beat 'em up, this time starring Marvel's mightiest.

I played through Marvel Cosmic Invasion multiple times and had a blast, but I moved on quickly, as I didn't feel the need to collect different palette-swaps of the many heroes on offer. Even after Cyclops and The Thing joined the roster as DLC in May, I still saw Cosmic Invasion as a game in the rearview. That changes this week, as The Siege of Castle Doom not only adds two additional playable characters (Invisible Woman and Doctor Doom), but also a mode that has the potential to bring me back for more runs for the foreseeable future.

Seeing that Annihilus is threatening the universe, Doom decides to take matters into his own hands. Unfortunately, much in the way that it seems that he may try to fix the multiversal incursions in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday, Victor Von Doom's solution in Marvel Cosmic Invasion – the Cosmic Inductor – would lead to untold death and destruction. In The Siege of Castle Doom, you select your team and fight your way through various floors of the stronghold belonging to the man who is perhaps Marvel's greatest villain. Your goal is to fight through the winding, randomized hallways of Castle Doomstadt, charging Reed Richards' Stabilizer and tactically bolstering your team along the way, before Doctor Doom can enact his plan.

It has been revealed that as for the upcoming playable characters, Doctor Doom is less agile, but his attacks pack a whallop, while Invisible Woman's force fields and speed make her the more versatile pick. I don't know that I see either of them replacing my mains from the base game, but I had fun experimenting with them throughout this mode. Regardless of which character you choose from the expanding roster, you still must traverse Castle Doomstadt before Doom achieves his objective.

In a recent development, fighting through waves of enemies across differently themed and booby-trapped rooms, you encounter all manner of foes from the base game, as well as latest minion types from Doom. When you defeat enemies, they drop batteries that charge your Stabilizer, letting you even the odds and stop Doom. Conversely, each time an enemy hits your character, it charges Doom's Cosmic Inductor, inching him closer to victory and making his minions faster and stronger in the process. As you might expect, the rooms get harder the deeper you go, and while each player starts with two characters to swap between, if a character completely depletes their health, they're gone for good, making it even tougher. As such, you need to keep your eyes on each character's health and swap them out when it makes sense.

As you complete each room, you can choose which path to take to augment your characters with upcoming special abilities. True to the roguelite structure, as you complete rooms, you can also buff your characters' stats within the run. Certain rooms offer extra batteries to help your Stabilizer charge, while others offer new and upgraded equipment. There's also one that promises random events that can easily alter the trajectory of your run for better or worse. Though I often enjoyed boosting attack stats to make enemies less like damage sponges, I had to balance that against buffing their health to keep them alive and charging the Stabilizer to have a fighting chance.

Beyond the in-run upgrades and modifiers, you can also amp up the action run-over-run through upgrades in Reed's Lab, which add to the pool of modifiers you can select from at the start of each run. The expansion also adds new palettes for existing heroes, plus new music by composer Tee Lopes. While I've only done a few runs of The Siege of Castle Doom (each taking between 45 and 90 minutes, depending on how successful you are), I feel a revitalized sense of excitement for Marvel Cosmic Invasion. Tribute claims completionists can spend upwards of 15 hours in this new mode, which has me champing at the bit to dive back into what will likely be my primary way of interacting with Marvel Cosmic Invasion going forward.

It has been revealed that marvel Cosmic Invasion – The Siege of Castle Doom is available today on all platforms, and it is a strong addition to an already great game. You can read our review of the base version of Marvel Cosmic Invasion here.
